## Abstract {.unnumbered}

\begingroup
\small

Arrayed reporter screens quantify microbial stress responses to chemical or
environmental perturbations. Their analysis is challenging because
reporter activity, growth, perturbation-wide shifts, background signal, plate
effects, and replicate structure are observed together. We introduce `DStressR`,
a statistical framework and R package for differential stress-response analysis
in such screens. The framework constructs or accepts an upstream response,
estimates reference-relative total effects and centered reporter-specific
deviations, and provides empirical-Bayes moderated tests and diagnostic
visualizations. Matched background reporters calibrate the response scale,
while technical covariates enter the effect model. Applications to public
*E. coli* luminescence and fluorescence screens demonstrate response-scale
estimation, effect-matrix diagnostics, and differential-response inference
across diverse screen designs. `DStressR` provides an extensible route from
arrayed reporter measurements to statistically transparent
stress-response maps.

\endgroup

## Author Summary {.unnumbered}

Reporter screens measure how bacterial stress-response reporters react to many
compounds, stresses, or other perturbations. Such data are powerful but
difficult to interpret, because reporter activity is entangled with growth,
perturbation-wide effects, technical variation, and background signal.
`DStressR` provides a reproducible R workflow for separating these components
and identifying reporter-perturbation responses that stand out from the broader
behaviour of the screen. Applications to public *E. coli* luminescence and
fluorescence assays compare model-based analysis with published hit-calling
workflows and decompose global and reporter-relative response structure.

## Introduction

Quantitative analysis of microbial responses to chemical perturbation is
essential for understanding bacterial physiology, antibiotic action, and
drug-microbe interactions [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Klobucar2018FEMS]. Modern robotics and plate-reader platforms allow these
responses to be measured at large scale, often by crossing compound collections
with strain libraries, species panels, or promoter reporters
[@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol; @Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow;
@Doherty2023ChemGAPP]. In bacteria, arrayed mutant collections and
high-throughput phenotyping have mapped genetic-interaction structure and
condition-dependent phenotypes in *Escherichia coli* [@Typas2008NatMethods;
@Nichols2011Cell]. Related chemical-genomics platforms further quantify
condition-specific fitness and chemical sensitivity across whole libraries
[@French2016ChemicalGenomics; @Kritikos2017Iris], classifying antibiotic
interactions, suppressive drug responses, species-specific combinations, and
resistance mechanisms [@Yeh2006NatGenet; @Bollenbach2009Cell;
@Brochado2018Nature; @Cacace2023NatMicrobiol; @Brenzinger2024NatMicrobiol].

Large-scale compound screens have similarly become central in microbiome and
chemical-genomics research [@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol;
@Klobucar2018FEMS]. Studies of human gut bacteria show that non-antibiotic drugs
inhibit growth, therapeutic compounds are bioaccumulated by cells, and
community-level behaviors emerge upon treatment [@Maier2018Nature;
@Klunemann2021Nature; @GarciaSantamarina2024Cell]. Systematic reporter
screening further maps how regulatory perturbations contribute to chemical cues,
virulence, antibiotic sensitivity, and stress-regulatory programs
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol; @Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen;
@Zannoni2026CampylobacterDrugScreen]. Beyond bacteria, chemical-genetic
profiling in yeast established foundational design principles for using
perturbation profiles to infer gene function and compound modes of action
[@Giaever2004PNAS; @Parsons2006Cell; @Hoon2008NatChemBiol;
@Hillenmeyer2008Science].

A complementary line of research stems from fluorescence promoter reporters, where
real-time green fluorescent protein (GFP) traces and biomass measurements
quantify gene expression dynamics in living bacteria [@Kalir2001Flagella;
@Ronen2002SOS; @Zaslaver2004JustInTime]. These methods expanded to
genome-scale *E. coli* promoter libraries [@Zaslaver2006ReporterLibrary] and
robotic assays linking promoter-activity distributions to growth physiology,
global regulation, and condition-specific promoter-activity deviations
[@Zaslaver2009PromoterDistribution; @Berthoumieux2013SharedControl;
@Gerosa2013SpecificGlobal; @Keren2013PromoterScaling;
@Rothschild2014LinearSuperposition; @Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling].

![Overview of a large-scale reporter-screen design. Reporter strains and a compound/stressor
collection are combined in an arrayed screen, producing hit-determination inputs for DStressR and growth-response curves 
for DGrowthR [@DGrowthR].](../figures/reporter_screen_overview.png){#fig-overview width="80%" fig-pos="t"}

The physical scale and geometry of these assays introduce structured technical
variation, including plate borders, row and column effects, robotic dispensing
patterns, and batch drift [@French2016ChemicalGenomics; @Kritikos2017Iris;
@Dittmar2010ScreenMill; @Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow]. Upstream
packages such as ScreenMill, Iris, gitter, and ChemGAPP handle image
processing, spatial correction, and growth summarization [@Dittmar2010ScreenMill;
@Kritikos2017Iris; @Wagih2014Gitter; @Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow;
@Doherty2023ChemGAPP]. Stress-response screens require an explicit
inferential target to separate reporter activity from growth and global
perturbation shifts. Making statistical targets, normalizations, and uncertainty
models explicit follows successful precedents from high-dimensional expression analysis
such as `limma` [@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Ritchie2015limma], `edgeR`
[@Robinson2010edgeR], and `DESeq2` [@Love2014DESeq2].

Here, we introduce `DStressR`, a statistical R framework and package designed
for differential perturbation-response analysis in arrayed screens. Several
workflows exist for microbial growth-curve modeling
[@Sprouffske2016Growthcurver; @Angaroni2025Kinbiont; @DGrowthR]. `DStressR`
focuses on differential effect estimation, shrinkage-stabilized response
scaling, empirical-Bayes variance moderation, and reproducible hit
determination with diagnostic tools. Chemical perturbations can alter
growth, metabolism, or signal intensity across the reporter library
[@Brochado2013CurrOpinMicrobiol; @Maier2018Nature;
@Brochado2018Nature; @Klunemann2021Nature; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP].
DStressR quantifies reference-relative responses and their departures from the
perturbation-wide average.

We analyze two public *E. coli* datasets. First, we consider a
large luminescence promoter-compound screen with matched empty-vector controls
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], comparing response construction and hit calls with the
published workflow. Second, we use a high-density fluorescence promoter-reporter
screen from the PFIbox study [@French2018PFIbox], analyzing image-derived
promoter-activity time series. In supplementary applications, DStressR recovers
the global growth-associated regulatory axis described by
@Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling and estimates window-specific fluorescence responses
with response-scale estimation from a separate no-stress reporter panel
[@Dash2024GlobalRegulators] (Suppl. Notes I.1--I.2). The datasets span
common screen geometries, ranging from small reporter panels
measured against many perturbations to large reporter libraries measured
under a smaller set of perturbation conditions (see Suppl. Table 1), thus
illustrating the scalability and versatility of the `DStressR` framework. The
manuscript and all analyses are fully reproducible and available on GitHub
<https://github.com/muellsen/DStressR>.

## Statistical Framework {#sec-statistical-framework}

### Overview of the Statistical Workflow

The analysis proceeds through statistically distinct operations
(@fig-statistical-workflow). We first define the experimental units, the
reporter and growth summaries, the reference conditions, and the technical
covariates that describe the screen. We then construct or supply an
observation-level response from paired reporter/growth measurements or from an
upstream activity estimator. This response can be further calibrated with a
matched background reporter, such as an empty-vector control, when such
measurements are available.

The model estimates reference-relative reporter-perturbation effects while
accounting for technical covariates. These total effects are the default
inferential target. Centering them across reporters within each perturbation
gives reporter-relative deviations from the panel average.
Optional low-rank adjustment acts on the fitted total-effect matrix
when latent structured background is analyzed. Uncertainty is quantified with
ordinary or moderated $t$-statistics and false-discovery-rate control.

![Statistical workflow implemented by DStressR. Reporter and growth summaries are first mapped to a response scale; optional background-reporter calibration acts on this response before model fitting. The downstream layers estimate reference-relative reporter-perturbation effects, center them into reporter-relative contrasts, optionally remove latent structured background, moderate uncertainty, control false discovery rates, and return directional hit calls.](../figures/Figure2-cropped.pdf){#fig-statistical-workflow width="95%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

### Experimental Design and Dimensions

We assume that raw reporter and growth time courses, colony traces, or
processed activity summaries have been reduced to one scalar input per retained
assay observation, possibly after upstream filtering such as replicate
concordance selection. We consider an arrayed screen crossing $n$ reporters
with $p$ non-reference perturbation levels. In microbial chemical-genomics
screens, reporters are often promoter-reporter strains and perturbations are
compounds [@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP;
@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. Perturbations may also represent stresses, pH conditions,
nutrients, or other assay-defined treatments. Let
$\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_n\}$ denote the reporter set and
$\mathcal C=\{1,\ldots,p\}$ the index set of non-reference perturbation levels.

In a balanced representation, each reporter has $r$ replicate measurements and
hence $N=nr$ reporter-replicate units. Each unit is measured against the $p$
non-reference perturbation levels and against $p_0$ reference conditions, usually DMSO, water,
or another assay-appropriate negative control specified by the analyst. Here
$n,p,r,p_0,N\in\mathbb N$. If rows index reporter-replicate units and columns
index the physical assay conditions, consisting of the $p$ non-reference
perturbation columns and the $p_0$ reference columns, the reporter and growth
summaries can be viewed as matrices

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:balanced-reporter-growth-matrices}
\mathcal L=(\mathcal L_{uh}),\quad
\mathcal G=(\mathcal G_{uh})
  \in
  \mathbb R^{N\times(p+p_0)},
  \qquad
  u=1,\ldots,N,\quad h=1,\ldots,p+p_0 .
\end{equation}

In Eq.\eqref{eq:balanced-reporter-growth-matrices},
$\mathcal L_{uh}$ and $\mathcal G_{uh}$ are the reporter and growth
summaries for reporter-replicate unit $u$ in physical assay column $h$. In
colony-array experiments, rows instead represent repeated spatial assay units.
For analysis, the retained matrix entries are unfolded into a long-format
table with rows $i=1,\ldots,M$: $u_i$ and $h_i$ identify the corresponding
assay unit and physical assay column, and $l_i=\mathcal L_{u_i h_i}$ and
$g_i=\mathcal G_{u_i h_i}$ are the observed summaries. This representation
retains the plate, batch, day, and replicate context of each control
observation and accommodates incomplete filtered designs.

The primary reporter measurement $l_i$ and growth measurement $g_i$ are positive
time-series summaries. They may be endpoint measurements at a fixed analysis
time $t^\star$, for example $l_i=\ell_i(t^\star)$ and
$g_i=\gamma_i(t^\star)$, Area-Under-the-Curve (AUC) summaries over a fixed
window, or quantities from an upstream time-series model, such as fitted
endpoint biomass or other growth-curve summaries [@DGrowthR]. Note that in some applications,
including promoter-activity (PA) workflows [@Zaslaver2006ReporterLibrary],
the upstream processing only provides a scalar response that effectively combines
reporter and growth measurements into a single quantity.

The same row carries reporter index $a_i\in\mathcal A$, modeled condition
$j_i\in\{0\}\cup\mathcal C$ induced by $h_i$, and encoded technical
covariates $x_i\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, such as plate, batch, day, or replicate
effects; $j_i=0$ denotes the assay reference class. The unit index
$u_i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$ identifies either a true replicate, representing an
independent experimental realization, or a repeated spatial measurement of
the same reporter construct, as specified by the experimental metadata. The
covariates $x_i$ adjust for this structure in the linear model. A complete
filtered design has $M=N(p+p_0)$ rows, although upstream filtering may make the
table incomplete. The observed data are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:observed-data}
\mathcal{D}
  =
  \left\{
    \left(l_i, g_i, u_i, a_i, j_i, x_i\right)
    : i=1,\ldots,M
\right\},
\end{equation}

The long-format data in Eq.\eqref{eq:observed-data} lead to an inferential
output that is naturally an $n\times p$ matrix of
reporter-perturbation contrasts, one entry for each reporter and non-control
perturbation.

### Response Construction

We construct a growth-adjusted response from paired reporter and growth
summaries or use a scalar activity response supplied by an upstream estimator.
A matched background reporter, such as an empty-vector control, provides
optional response calibration.

#### Model Definition

For paired summaries from retained observation $i=1,\ldots,M$, let

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:log-summary-scale}
\begin{aligned}
L_i
  &=
  \log_2 (l_i+\epsilon),
&
G_i
  &=
  \log_2 (g_i+\epsilon).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The pseudo-count $\epsilon\geq 0$ is a numerical safeguard for zero or
near-zero summaries. The package default is $\epsilon=10^{-8}$, while
$\epsilon=0$ can be used when all retained summaries are strictly positive.
The ordinary log reporter-to-growth ratio $L_i-G_i$ corresponds to fixed ratio
normalization with $\alpha=1$. DStressR generalizes this construction by
allowing a reporter-specific growth exponent:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:response-scale}
\begin{aligned}
y_i
  &=
  L_i
  -
  \alpha_{a_i}G_i.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

When the pseudo-count is small relative to the measured signal, this response
in Eq.\eqref{eq:response-scale} has the approximation $y_i \approx
\log_2\{l_i/g_i^{\alpha_{a_i}}\}$. Multiplicative coupling between reporter
and growth summaries becomes additive on this working log scale, allowing
linear models to estimate growth-adjusted perturbation effects with technical
covariate adjustment.

Fluorescence promoter-activity workflows often define the response by
background-correcting fluorescence, normalizing by biomass, and differentiating
or integrating the resulting time series [@Zaslaver2006ReporterLibrary;
@Gerosa2013SpecificGlobal; @French2018PFIbox]. Such a promoter-activity
summary enters DStressR as a supplied response $y_i^\star$ for effect
estimation and testing.

The exponent may be fixed at $\alpha_a=1$ for ordinary ratio normalization. The
default DStressR analysis estimates reporter-specific exponents from
reference observations and stabilizes them by shrinkage. Externally specified
exponents can be used in the same response equation.

#### Growth-Exponent Estimation

When $\alpha_a$ is estimated, `DStressR` uses only reference observations,
e.g., DMSO, water, or other user-defined controls. We denote the observed
reference observations by $\mathcal I_0=\{i:j_i=0\}$ and use the
log-transformed quantities $L_i$ and $G_i$ defined in
Eq.\eqref{eq:log-summary-scale}. This step is skipped when the response is
supplied directly by an upstream activity estimator.

For reporter $a$, the raw growth exponent is the slope from the regression on
$\mathcal I_a^0=\{i\in\mathcal I_0:a_i=a\}$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-growth-slope}
L_i
  =
  \eta_a
  +
  \alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}G_i
  +
  z_i^\top\theta_a
  +
  \xi_i,
  \qquad i\in\mathcal I_a^0 .
\end{equation}

Here $z_i\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$ contains the technical covariates selected for
response-scale estimation, with coefficient vector
$\theta_a\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$, while
$\eta_a,\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}},\xi_i\in\mathbb R$. These covariates account
for the contexts in which reference observations are measured and may differ
from the covariates $x_i$ used for effect estimation.

A global reference slope is also estimated from all reference observations by fitting

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:global-growth-slope}
L_i
  =
  \eta
  +
  \alpha_0 G_i
  +
  \rho^{(0)}_{a_i}
  +
  z_i^\top\theta
  +
  \xi_i.
\end{equation}

Here $z_i,\theta\in\mathbb R^{d_z}$ and
$\eta,\alpha_0,\rho^{(0)}_{a_i},\xi_i\in\mathbb R$. The reporter-specific
intercept adjustment $\rho^{(0)}_{a_i}$ is encoded with an identifiable
contrast because the model contains the intercept $\eta$. DStressR stabilizes
usable reporter-specific slopes by shrinking them toward the global slope,
following the empirical-Bayes principle used in high-throughput genomic assays
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Love2014DESeq2]. Let $\widehat s_a^2$ denote the squared
standard error of $\widehat\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}$, and let
$\widehat\tau^2$ denote a positive estimate of between-reporter exponent
variance after subtracting a typical sampling variance. The shrunken exponent
is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:shrunk-growth-exponent}
\widehat\alpha_a
  =
  \frac{
    \widehat\alpha_a^{\mathrm{raw}}/\widehat s_a^2
    +
    \widehat\alpha_0/\widehat\tau^2
  }{
    1/\widehat s_a^2
    +
    1/\widehat\tau^2
  }.
\end{equation}

Reporters without a usable raw slope use the global slope. The default response
model uses the shrunken exponent $\widehat\alpha_a$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:shrunk-growth-exponent}, yielding the observation-level response
$\widehat y_i=L_i-\widehat\alpha_{a_i}G_i$; final exponents are clipped to
$[-2,3]$ unless clipping is disabled.

#### Background Reporter Calibration

DStressR distinguishes a condition reference, such as DMSO or water, from a
reporter-background reference, such as an empty-vector control. The condition
reference defines the treatment contrast between non-control perturbations and the
within-reporter baseline. A background reporter can calibrate the response
scale before effect estimation. Let $e$ denote the
background reporter and let $b_i$ be the matched background response for
observation $i$, matched on perturbation and, where available, concentration,
plate, batch, or replicate. For reporter $a\ne e$, let
$\mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}}$ denote the set of matched, finite observations for that
reporter; equivalently, $a=a_i$ for observations in this set. The
response-level calibration model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-calibration}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat y_i
  &=
  \gamma_{0a}
  +
  \gamma_{1a} b_i
  +
  \varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{bg}},
  \qquad i\in\mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}},\ a\ne e .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $b_i,\gamma_{0a},\gamma_{1a},\varepsilon_i^{\mathrm{bg}}\in\mathbb R$.
Calibration uses ordinary least squares or reporter-wise Huber robust
regression. The latter follows the calibration used in the original *E. coli*
analysis [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol] and estimates the coefficients with Huber's
loss [@Huber1981RobustStatistics]. For each reporter $a\ne e$, the robust
coefficients solve

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-huber-objective}
  (\widehat\gamma_{0a},\widehat\gamma_{1a})
  =
  \arg\min_{\gamma_0,\gamma_1}
  \sum_{i \in \mathcal I_a^{\mathrm{bg}}}
  \rho_H\!\left(
    \frac{\widehat y_i - \gamma_0 - \gamma_1 b_i}{\widehat\sigma_a^{\mathrm{bg}}}
  \right),
\end{equation}

where $\rho_H(\cdot)$ is the Huber loss with tuning constant 1.345 and
$\widehat\sigma_a^{\mathrm{bg}}>0$ is the fitted residual scale. The
implementation uses the iteratively updated, rescaled median absolute
deviation of residuals in `MASS::rlm`; the objective is evaluated at the
converged scale. The calibrated response is the residual

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:background-reporter-residual}
\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}
  =
  \widehat y_i
  -
  \left(
    \widehat\gamma_{0a_i}
    +
    \widehat\gamma_{1a_i} b_i
  \right),
\end{equation}

and the background reporter is removed from the tested reporter set. This
calibration estimates reporter-specific background coupling through
$\gamma_{1a}$.

Following @Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen, baseline background subtraction
is the special case $\gamma_{0a}=0$ and $\gamma_{1a}=1$, yielding
$\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}=\widehat y_i-b_i$.

The response vector passed to differential analysis is therefore
$\mathbf y^\star=(y_1^\star,\ldots,y_M^\star)^\top\in\mathbb R^M$, with
$y_i^\star=\widehat y_i$ for the uncalibrated response and
$y_i^\star=\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-residual} for the background-calibrated
response.

### Estimands

#### Total and Reporter-relative Effects

We next define the estimands on the constructed (or supplied) response scale
$y_i^\star$. Let $\mathcal A^\star$ be the tested reporter set, with size
$n^\star$. Usually $\mathcal A^\star=\mathcal A$; when a background reporter is
used for response calibration, that reporter is excluded from
$\mathcal A^\star$. Because the analysis may include plate, batch, day,
replicate, or other technical covariates, reporter-perturbation responses are
defined at a common technical covariate setting $x^\star\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$.
For reporter
$a\in\mathcal A^\star$ and perturbation or reference condition $j$, write

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:standardized-mean-response}
\begin{aligned}
\mu_y(a,j;x^\star)
  &=
  \operatorname{E}
  \left(
    y_i^\star
    \mid
    a_i=a,\ j_i=j,\ x_i=x^\star
  \right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The reference condition, indexed by $0$, defines the within-reporter baseline.
In applications, this may be a solvent/reference control such as DMSO, water,
or another assay-appropriate negative control. For reporter
$a\in\mathcal A^\star$ and perturbation $j\in\mathcal C$, the reference-relative
total effect, our default target of inference, is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \mu_y(a,j;x^\star)
  -
  \mu_y(a,0;x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

To identify responses that depart from the reporter-panel average, we
decompose total effects into a perturbation-wide mean and reporter-relative
deviations. For perturbation $j$, the library-wide average response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:compound-wide-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n^\star}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The reporter-relative effect quantifies a deviation from the mean total effect
across the tested reporters for the same perturbation. We subtract the library-wide component in
Eq.\eqref{eq:compound-wide-effect}:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reporter-relative-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This centering removes an additive perturbation effect shared across the tested
reporters. It follows the background-removal principle of median polish
(Supplementary Note B.1), with reporter baselines and technical effects
estimated by regression and perturbation-wide shifts estimated by averaging.
Median polish estimates row and column effects by alternating median subtraction.

#### Adjustment for Latent Factors

We represent structured perturbation-wide variation by a latent low-rank
background with reporter-dependent contributions.
Let $T\in\mathbb R^{n^\star\times p}$ denote the reference-relative total
effect matrix with entries $T_{aj}=\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$. For a
specified rank $k$, define the low-rank background matrix as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:low-rank-background-estimand}
\begin{aligned}
B^{(k)}
  &=
  \arg\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb R^{n^\star\times p}\\
                      \operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \sum_{j\in\mathcal C}
  \left(
    T_{aj}
    -
    B_{aj}
  \right)^2 .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The rank-adjusted total-effect estimand is then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rank-adjusted-total-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  B^{(k)}_{aj}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

If a reporter-relative effect is desired after rank adjustment, it
is obtained by centering the rank-adjusted total effects within perturbation:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rank-adjusted-reporter-relative-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel},k}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  -
  \frac{1}{n^\star}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A^\star}
  \Delta y_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot},k}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The default analysis uses $k=0$, for which $B^{(0)}=0$ and
Eq.\eqref{eq:rank-adjusted-reporter-relative-effect} reduces to
Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect}. Positive ranks, typically $k=1$ or $k=2$, are
used when the fitted total-effect matrix shows structured background
variation. We diagnose this structure by permutation parallel analysis: the
observed singular values of $T$ are compared with singular values obtained
after independently permuting reporter labels within each perturbation column.
This preserves perturbation-wise marginal effect distributions while breaking
coherent reporter-loading structure. The diagnostic follows parallel analysis
[@Horn1965ParallelAnalysis] and its permutation interpretation
[@BujaEyuboglu1992ParallelAnalysis], with modern theoretical support from
permutation-based PCA diagnostics [@Dobriban2017PermutationPCA] and
deterministic refinements [@DobribanOwen2019DeterministicParallelAnalysis].
Missing entries are replaced by the observed perturbation-column mean for the
singular-value decomposition; inference is reported only for fitted
reporter-perturbation pairs. The rank can be specified by the analyst or
selected by this diagnostic.

### Model-Based Inference {#sec-model-based-inference}

#### Linear Model

The filtered data $\mathcal D$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:observed-data} estimate the
conditional means in Eq.\eqref{eq:standardized-mean-response}. For large-scale
screens, we fit one Gaussian linear model per reporter, which gives a scalable
decomposition of the reporter-perturbation effect matrix. For reporter $a$, define
$\mathcal I_a=\{i:a_i=a\}$. On this set $a=a_i$, and the working model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-specific-working-model}
\begin{aligned}
y_i^\star
  &=
  \mu_a
  +
  \delta_{a,j_i}
  +
  x_i^\top\gamma_a
  +
  \varepsilon_i,
  \qquad
  i\in\mathcal I_a,\quad
  \varepsilon_i\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\sigma_a^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $\mu_a,\delta_{a,j_i},\varepsilon_i\in\mathbb R$,
$x_i,\gamma_a\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, $\sigma_a^2>0$, $\mu_a$ is the
reporter-specific baseline, $\delta_{a,j_i}$ is the perturbation effect within
reporter $a$, and $x_i^\top\gamma_a$ adjusts for technical covariates within
that reporter. The reference condition has
$\delta_{a,0}=0$ under the usual reference coding. The normal model is a
working sampling model for the constructed response $y_i^\star$.
If an ordered or quantitative design column, such as a concentration index, is
included in $x_i$, its systematic contribution is adjusted as a numeric
nuisance covariate. Categorical technical variables, such as replicate or plate
labels, enter through their corresponding indicator columns. The reported
$\delta_{a,j}$ in Eq.\eqref{eq:promoter-specific-working-model} then
represents the covariate-adjusted effect of perturbation $j$ for reporter $a$.

In matrix notation for reporter $a$, with $m_a=|\mathcal I_a|$ retained rows,
$\mathbf y_a^\star,\varepsilon_a\in\mathbb R^{m_a}$,
$X_a\in\mathbb R^{m_a\times d_a}$, and
$\beta_a\in\mathbb R^{d_a}$, we write

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:promoter-specific-matrix-model}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}^{\star}_a
  &=
  X_a\beta_a
  +
  \varepsilon_a,
  \\
  \varepsilon_{a,i}
  &\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
  \mathcal N(0,\sigma_a^2).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Here $X_a$ contains an intercept, perturbation indicators, and the selected
technical covariates for reporter $a$. For small perturbation
panels, the same scalar target can also be estimated from a full interaction
model. With
$\mathbf y^\star,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^M$,
$X_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^{M\times d_{\mathrm{int}}}$, and
$\beta_{\mathrm{int}}\in\mathbb R^{d_{\mathrm{int}}}$, this model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:optional-interaction-model}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{y}^{\star}
  &=
  X_{\mathrm{int}}\beta_{\mathrm{int}}
  +
  \varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}},
  \\
  \varepsilon_{\mathrm{int},i}
  &\overset{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}
  \mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\mathrm{int}}^2),
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $X_{\mathrm{int}}$ contains reporter, perturbation, reporter-perturbation
interaction, and technical-covariate terms.

#### Estimation of Total and Reporter-relative Effects

For estimation from Eq.\eqref{eq:promoter-specific-matrix-model}, we write
$m_a(j,x^\star)\in\mathbb R^{d_a}$ for the row of
$X_a$ corresponding to perturbation $j$ and the reference technical covariate
setting $x^\star$ in the reporter-specific model for reporter $a$. The fitted
standardized mean is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:fitted-standardized-mean}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\mu}_y(a,j;x^\star)
  &=
  m_a(j,x^\star)^\top
  \widehat{\beta}_{a}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Thus the total-effect contrast that estimates Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect} is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-effect-contrast}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  m_a(j,x^\star)
  -
  m_a(0,x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The estimated total effect and its model-based standard error are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:total-contrast-estimate}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \left(\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^\top
  \widehat{\beta}_{a},
  \\
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \left(\Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^\top
  \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\beta}_{a})
  \Delta m_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

For perturbation $j$, let $\mathcal A_j$ be the set of tested reporters with an
estimated total effect and let $n_j=|\mathcal A_j|$. The perturbation-wide and
reporter-relative estimates are then computed as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:implemented-global-relative-estimates}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_j}
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
  &=
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}} .
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This averaging and subtraction is applied for each perturbation across its tested
reporters. Low-rank background adjustment applies a rank-$k$ singular-value
approximation to the total-effect matrix with entries
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$, giving the rank-adjusted total
estimate
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
=\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat B^{(k)}_{aj}$.

The corresponding rank-adjusted reporter-relative estimate is obtained by centering
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}$ across reporters within perturbation.
With $k=0$, $\widehat B^{(0)}_{aj}=0$ and both estimates reduce to their
unadjusted counterparts.

Under the reporter-wise fitting decomposition, the variance of the
reporter-relative effect estimate is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reporter-relative-effect-variance}
\begin{aligned}
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
  &=
  \left(\frac{n_j-1}{n_j}\right)^2
  v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  +
  \frac{1}{n_j^2}
  \sum_{a'\in\mathcal A_j,\ a'\ne a}
  v_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \\
s_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
  &=
  \sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

#### Additive Empty-Vector Adjustment

We formulate a model-based analogue of the background subtraction used by
@Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen by subtracting fitted empty-vector
contrasts from reporter total effects. We retain the empty-vector observations
in the effect model and use responses without response-level background
calibration. Let $e$
denote the empty-vector reporter; the tested reporter set is
$\mathcal A^\star$, excluding $e$. For each perturbation, the fitted
empty-vector response is the reference-relative contrast

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-effect}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  &=
  \mu_y(e,j;x^\star)
  -
  \mu_y(e,0;x^\star).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

We define the background-adjusted total effect by subtracting this fitted
empty-vector contrast from the reporter-level total effect:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-total}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

This contrast measures the perturbation-induced change in the reporter
relative to the corresponding change in the empty-vector control. Under the
cross-reporter independence approximation, its variance is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-variance}
\begin{aligned}
v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  +
  v_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}},
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

where $v_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}$ is the model-based variance of
the empty-vector contrast in Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-effect}.
We use the adjusted total effect and this variance for inference on
background-adjusted responses, with Welch--Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
$\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}=(v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}})^2/
\{(v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}})^2/\nu_a+(v_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}})^2/\nu_e\}$,
where $\nu_a$ and $\nu_e$ are the residual degrees of freedom of the reporter
and empty-vector fits [@Satterthwaite1946; @Welch1947].

For reporter-relative effects, we additionally center over the tested
reporters. Let $\mathcal A_j$ be the set of tested reporters with a fitted
effect for perturbation $j$, and let $n_j=|\mathcal A_j|$. Their
background-adjusted mean is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:model-empty-vector-centering}
\begin{aligned}
\overline{\Delta y}_{j}^{\mathrm{adj}}
  &=
  \frac{1}{n_j}
  \sum_{a\in\mathcal A_j}
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Because the additive background shift $\Delta y_{ej}^{\mathrm{evc}}$ enters
every adjusted reporter response for perturbation $j$, it cancels during the
centering in Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-centering}. The resulting
reporter-relative contrast equals Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect} in a complete
design; an incomplete design uses the corresponding $n_j$-reporter mean.
The centered-effect variance remains Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect-variance}.

#### Standard Hypothesis Testing

For total-effect inference, we test
$H_{0,aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}:\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}=0$.
The default $k=0$ tests the reference-relative total effect in
Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}. Let $\nu_a$ denote the residual degrees of freedom
of the fitted reporter model. The ordinary statistic is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ordinary-rank-adjusted-total-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
t_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  &=
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}}
       {s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}},
  \qquad
t_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}
  \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
  \operatorname{t}_{\nu_a}
  \quad\text{under }H_{0,aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

For an additive empty-vector total-effect analysis, the numerator is the
adjusted effect in Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-total} and the
standard error is $\sqrt{v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-variance}, with
$\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}$ degrees of freedom.

For reporter-relative effect inference, we test
$H_{0,aj}:\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel},k}=0$.
Under the working independence assumption across reporter fits, the effective
degrees of freedom of the centered variance in
Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect-variance} are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:reporter-relative-effect-df}
\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
 = \frac{(v_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}})^2}
 {\left(\frac{n_j-1}{n_j}\right)^4
     (v_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}})^2/\nu_a
  + n_j^{-4}\sum_{a'\in\mathcal A_j,\ a'\ne a}
     (v_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}})^2/\nu_{a'}}.
\end{equation}

This approximation matches the first two moments of the sum of variance
components [@Satterthwaite1946; @Welch1947]. Effective-degree-of-freedom
approximations also support differential-expression analysis with mixed
models, including `dream` [@Hoffman2021dream]. The ordinary reporter-relative effect
statistic is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ordinary-t-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
t_{aj}
  &=
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel},k}}
       {s_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}},
  \qquad
t_{aj}
  \overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}
  \operatorname{t}_{\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}}
  \quad\text{under }H_{0,aj}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Response-level background calibration enters both targets through
$y_i^\star=\widehat y_i^{\mathrm{bg}}$. For the full interaction model, we use
its common residual degrees of freedom and joint coefficient covariance.
The contrast construction follows the design-matrix logic used in standard
differential-analysis workflows [@Smyth2004limmaEB; @McCarthy2012edgeRGLM;
@Love2014DESeq2].

#### Moderated Hypothesis Testing

DStressR uses empirical-Bayes variance moderation by default, borrowing
information across the complete set of fitted contrasts to stabilize their
uncertainty while preserving the estimated effects. For each tested
reporter-perturbation contrast
$\omega=(a,j)\in\mathcal A^\star\times\mathcal C$, let
$\widehat\Delta_\omega$ denote the selected numerator and $v_\omega$ its
model-based variance:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:contrast-variance-index}
\begin{aligned}
\widehat\Delta_\omega
  &=
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},k},
\\
v_\omega
  &=
  \left(s_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\right)^2,
\\
s_\omega
  &=
  \sqrt{v_\omega}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Eq.\eqref{eq:contrast-variance-index} is written for total effects, with
$k=0$ by default. For a reporter-relative effect analysis,
$\widehat\Delta_\omega=
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel},k}$ and
$v_\omega=(s_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}})^2$. For background-adjusted total effects,
we use $\widehat\Delta_\omega=\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-total} and
$v_\omega=v_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:model-empty-vector-adjusted-variance}. When $k>0$, inference is conditional on
the estimated low-rank background.

For reporter-wise fits, total-effect tests use $\nu_\omega=\nu_a$ and
reporter-relative effect tests use $\nu_\omega=\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect-df}. Background-adjusted total-effect tests use
$\nu_\omega=\nu_{aj}^{\mathrm{adj}}$; we combine their raw variance components
before moderation. Contrasts from the full interaction model use its common
residual degrees of freedom. We construct the reporter-relative effect variance from
the raw total-effect variances and moderate it once; total-effect moderation
is performed separately.

A common prior variance $s_0^2$ and prior degrees of freedom $\nu_0$ are
estimated from the empirical distribution of finite positive contrast
variances, following the empirical-Bayes variance-moderation logic of
differential-expression workflows [@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Ritchie2015limma].
The moment equations account for individual contrast degrees of freedom
(Supplementary Note C). This is a working approximation for centered contrasts,
whose variance estimates share reporter-level residual variances.
For each reporter-perturbation contrast, the moderated variance can be written
as a posterior-style average of the contrast-specific variance and the
empirical prior scale:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-variance}
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde v_\omega
  =
  \frac{\nu_\omega v_\omega + \widehat{\nu}_0 \widehat{s}_0^2}
       {\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Equivalently, with
$w_\omega=\nu_\omega/(\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0)$, the same moderation is
$\widetilde v_\omega = w_\omega v_\omega + (1-w_\omega)\widehat{s}_0^2$.

The moderated standard error and moderated $t$ statistic are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-standard-error-statistic}
\begin{aligned}
\widetilde s_\omega
  &=
  \sqrt{\widetilde v_\omega},\\[4pt]
\widetilde t_\omega
  &=
  \frac{\widehat\Delta_\omega}{\widetilde s_\omega}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

The two-sided moderated p-value is then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:moderated-pvalue}
\widetilde\pi_\omega
  =
  2\,\Pr
  \left\{
    \operatorname{t}_{\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0}
    \ge
    |\widetilde t_\omega|
  \right\}.
\end{equation}

#### Multiple Testing

Let $\Omega$ denote the fitted set of reporter-perturbation contrasts after
filtering. The model-based default treats $\Omega$ as one hypothesis family and
adjusts the moderated p-values globally with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
[@BenjaminiHochberg1995]. Reporter-wise adjusted p-values are also reported
for screen-specific hit-calling conventions.

## Analysis of an E. coli Promoter-Compound Screen

### Screen Data and Biological Scope

We first applied DStressR to the public *E. coli* promoter-reporter screen of
Binsfeld et al. [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. The screen uses a compact,
biologically structured reporter library centered on the Mar-Sox-Rob
stress-response and permeability network.
The tested promoters cover multidrug efflux (`acrABp`, `tolCp`),
transcriptional regulation by MarA, SoxS, and Rob (`marRABp`, `soxSp`,
`robp`), and outer-membrane permeability regulation through the MicF/OmpF axis
(`micFp`, `ompFp`). We estimate reference-relative total effects to characterize
changes in this connected regulatory panel, including coordinated responses
across several promoters. Reporter-relative effects describe each promoter's
departure from the panel average and are examined in Supplementary Note G.

The data comprise $M=5{,}894$ retained well summaries after quality-control filtering [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol],
$n^\star=7$ tested promoters, one empty-vector reporter $e=$ `EVC` for
optional background calibration, $p=94$ non-water compounds, with water as the
reference condition $j=0$. The design contains two replicate labels and four
concentration-index positions; water controls remain balanced with 16 retained
observations per reporter, while non-water cells are mildly unbalanced after
quality control. The resulting DStressR testing family contains
$n^\star p=7\times94=658$ reference-relative promoter-compound contrasts. The raw OD and
luminescence time series, derived AUC summaries, and published score and
Z-score summaries are publicly available ([@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], Supp.
Datasets 1--4, Supp. Tables 3--4). We use the WT AUC summaries for the
DStressR reanalysis and the published WT Z-score table to reconstruct the
reference hit-calling rule. Supplementary Note B defines two additional
published, screen-specific estimators retained for reproducibility: the
Campylobacter median-polish workflow and the Salmonella empty-vector-control
workflow. These estimators start from pre-normalized responses and aggregate
replicate-level evidence in wide promoter-compound screens
[@Zannoni2026CampylobacterDrugScreen; @Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen].

### Original Response Construction and Hit-Calling Workflow

The original workflow converts time-resolved OD and luminescence measurements into
reporter scores and calls hits from a Wilcoxon/BH procedure applied to
reporter-column Z-scores. Let $i\in\{1,\ldots,M\}$ index a
retained well summary, with promoter label $a_i$, compound label $j_i$, and
reporter column or replicate label $q_i$. Each WT
trajectory is summarized by its Area-Under-the-Curve (AUC) over the first 8 hours. 
We write the resulting growth AUC as $g_i$ and the luminescence AUC as $l_i$.
Wells with very low growth are removed by setting both summaries to missing 
when $g_i$ is less than 10% of the plate median. In the retained WT data, 
both AUC summaries are strictly positive.

The original Lux-growth response is the fixed ratio $R_i^{\mathrm{orig}}=l_i/g_i$. The original workflow uses this ratio on its observed scale and uses the empty-vector reporter as a background reference. The published code represents
the screen as a wide table with one column per
reporter-replicate and one row per well position. Let $h_i$ denote the well
position of observation $i$, let $q_i$ denote its reporter-replicate column,
and write $R_{hq}^{\mathrm{orig}}$ for the fixed-ratio response at well position $h$ and
column $q$. If $\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}$ denotes the set of EVC
reporter-replicate columns, the reference EVC profile is the row-wise average

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-evc-reference}
  e_h =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}|}
  \sum_{q\in\mathcal Q_{\mathrm{EVC}}} R_{hq}^{\mathrm{orig}}.
\end{equation}

For each reporter column $q$, the workflow fits a Huber calibration of the
reporter ratio on this shared EVC profile
[@Huber1981RobustStatistics; @Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol],

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-huber-fit}
  R_{hq}^{\mathrm{orig}} = \beta_{0q}+\beta_{1q}e_h+\xi_{hq},
  \qquad h\in\mathcal H_q,
\end{equation}

where $\mathcal H_q$ is the set of non-missing well positions in reporter
column $q$. The reported score is the residual

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-score}
  s_i =
  R_{h_iq_i}^{\mathrm{orig}} -
  \left(
    \widehat\beta_{0q_i}+\widehat\beta_{1q_i}e_{h_i}
  \right).
\end{equation}

For promoter-compound summaries on the original response scale, let
$\mathcal P_{aj}=\{i:a_i=a,\;j_i=j\}$ denote the retained wells for promoter
$a$ and compound $j$, and let $\mathcal P_{a0}$ denote the water controls for
that promoter. We define the corresponding mean residual score as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}
  \bar{s}_{aj}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal P_{aj}|}
  \sum_{i\in\mathcal P_{aj}}s_i .
\end{equation}

Following typical methodology in the field (@Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow), 
the residual scores in Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-score} are median-centered and
scaled within reporter column.
Let $\mathcal I_q=\{i:q_i=q\}$ denote the retained observations in reporter
column $q$. Then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-z-score}
  Z_i =
  \frac{s_i-\operatorname{median}_{m\in\mathcal I_{q_i}}(s_m)}
       {\operatorname{sd}_{m\in\mathcal I_{q_i}}(s_m)}.
\end{equation}

For hit calling, Z-scores are pooled across reporter replicates and
concentration-index positions. Using the same sets $\mathcal P_{aj}$ and
$\mathcal P_{a0}$, the published rule compares compound and water Z-scores
using a Wilcoxon rank-sum test,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-wilcox}
  p_{aj}^{\mathrm{ref}}
  =
  p_{\mathrm{Wilcoxon}}
  \left(
    \{Z_i:i\in\mathcal P_{aj}\},
    \{Z_i:i\in\mathcal P_{a0}\}
  \right).
\end{equation}

The p-values are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure within promoter
[@BenjaminiHochberg1995], yielding $q_{aj}^{\mathrm{BH,promoter}}$, and paired
with the mean pooled Z-score
$\overline Z_{aj}=|\mathcal P_{aj}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal P_{aj}}Z_i$. A
promoter-compound pair is called by the Binsfeld reference rule when

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binsfeld-style-hit-rule}
\mathrm{hit}_{aj}^{\mathrm{ref}}
  =
  \left\{
    q_{aj}^{\mathrm{BH,promoter}}<0.05
  \right\}
  \cap
  \left\{
    |\overline Z_{aj}|>1
  \right\}.
\end{equation}

### Default DStressR Workflows

The DStressR reanalysis uses water as reference condition (16
observations per reporter). Since all retained Lux and OD AUC values are positive, 
the log response scale in Eq.\eqref{eq:response-scale} requires no
pseudo-count (i.e., $\epsilon=0$). In this application,
$y_i=\log_2(l_i)-\widehat\alpha_{a_i}\log_2(g_i)$, where $l_i$ and
$g_i$ are Lux and OD AUC summaries. The promoter-specific growth-response
exponents are estimated from water controls with replicate adjustment and
shrunken toward a global water-control slope.

We analyze two model-based variants, distinguished by
whether the empty-vector control (EVC) is used for background calibration. DStressR
without EVC uses this growth-modeled response directly. DStressR with EVC first constructs
the growth-modeled response for all reporters and then calibrates each tested
promoter against the matched empty-vector response using the Huber
background-calibration model in
Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-calibration}.

The downstream model adjusts for replicate and concentration-index position.
Because the source index increases with dilution, we use a reversed coding
$\mathrm{dose\_level}=5-\mathrm{concentration\_index}$ so that larger values
denote higher concentration for non-water wells; for water controls, the same
column records matched layout position. Both variants report one covariate-adjusted
total effect per promoter-compound pair using Eq.\eqref{eq:total-contrast-estimate}.
We test these total effects using Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue}, with the
total-effect numerator and variance specified in
Eq.\eqref{eq:contrast-variance-index} and $k=0$. We use no low-rank adjustment
and apply Benjamini-Hochberg correction within promoter at FDR 0.05. The
original rule additionally requires the Z-score cutoff in
Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-style-hit-rule}.

### Results

**Response-scale construction.** We first compared DStressR's response modeling
with the original Lux/growth ratio (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction).
The estimated reporter-specific control-well Lux-growth slopes are largest for `micFp` and `ompFp` 
and smallest for `acrABp` and `tolCp` (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction a), respectively. 
With 16 water-control observations per reporter, shrinkage pulls
these estimates toward the global water-control slope,
$\widehat\alpha_0\approx0.379$, yielding closely grouped exponents below the
fixed-ratio value $\alpha_a=1$. The matched EVC
calibration remains reporter-specific: Huber slopes range from 0.25 for
`marRABp` to 0.99 for `robp` (@fig-binsfeld-response-construction b), 
so the contribution of the matched background signal varies across reporters.

We next compare the DStressR responses with the original promoter-compound
response $\bar{s}_{aj}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}
(@fig-binsfeld-response-construction c,d). Since this response is signed and
defined on a linear scale, we show $\bar{s}_{aj}$ on a pseudo log-scale. We observed
that DStressR changes the response geometry through promoter-specific growth
scaling and EVC calibration. The corresponding response distributions are shown
in Suppl. Figure 1.

The dashed vertical line marks $\alpha_a=1$ and the dotted vertical line marks the global water-control slope $\widehat\alpha_0$. Panel b shows reporter-specific EVC calibration slopes $\widehat\gamma_{1a}$ from the Huber calibration model in Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-calibration}--Eq.\eqref{eq:background-reporter-huber-objective}; the EVC row is empty because the EVC reporter serves as the calibration reference. Panels c and d compare promoter-compound responses after DStressR response construction with the original response $\bar{s}_{aj}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-mean-score}, shown on a pseudo log-scale, without and with EVC, respectively.](../../analysis/outputs/binsfeld_modeling_steps/binsfeld_response_modeling_combined.png){#fig-binsfeld-response-construction width="50%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="H"}

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}

**Effect-matrix estimation and diagnostics.** We next estimated total
promoter-compound effects under both model-based variants
(@fig-binsfeld-effect-matrix-diagnostic a,b). The fitted total effects
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:total-contrast-estimate} highlight compounds that shift several
promoters in the same direction. EVC calibration changes selected effects but
preserves the broad structure of the total-effect matrix.

To summarize the variability of the total effect of a compound on the set of promoters, we use an effect-matrix diagnostic that reduces each column of the total-effect matrix from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-contrast-estimate} to its average fitted total response and its variance across promoters. For each compound, we ranked the absolute mean total response
$|\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}|$ and compared it with the
variance of the fitted total effects
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ across promoters
(@fig-binsfeld-effect-matrix-diagnostic c,d). This display distinguishes compounds
that shift the reporter library coherently from compounds with heterogeneous
promoter-level responses. In the *E. coli* screen, most compounds have small
promoter-wise variance. PMS, Clarithromycin, Azithromycin, Procaine, and
Paraquat show stronger promoter heterogeneity on top of their fitted
compound-level responses.

Panels c and d summarize the same total-effect matrices by ranking compounds according to $|\widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}|$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:implemented-global-relative-estimates} and plotting the variance of $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ across promoters. \Needspace{3\baselineskip}

**Hit-calling comparison.** We next tested which compounds changed promoter
activity relative to water, using the total effects
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:total-contrast-estimate} and moderated p-values from
Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue}. We compared these calls with the published
Wilcoxon analysis of standardized well scores $Z_i$
(Eq.\eqref{eq:binsfeld-wilcox}; @fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary).
All three analyses use within-promoter BH adjustment at 0.05; the published
rule also requires $|\overline Z_{aj}|>1$. The p-value distributions show an
enrichment near zero across the three workflows
(@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary a--c).

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}

We identified 145 significant promoter-compound pairs without EVC calibration
and 119 with EVC calibration, compared with 53 under the published rule.
Thirty-five pairs were shared by all three analyses. The two DStressR
variants shared 104 pairs, including 69 additional to the published set
(@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary g). The union comprised 171 pairs
(Suppl. Table 2), with method-specific calls shown in
@fig-binsfeld-discovery-summary h--i. For total-effect moderation, we estimated
$\widehat\nu_0=7.66$ without EVC and $\widehat\nu_0=11.34$ with EVC, with
reporter-model residual degrees of freedom ranging from 626 to 652 and
625 to 646, respectively. Moderation reduced the call counts from 147 to 145
and from 120 to 119. Promoter-wise p-value distributions and complete hit
lists are provided in Suppl. Figure 2 and Suppl. Tables 2--3.

We recovered responses across the redox, permeability, and efflux pathways
represented in the reporter panel.

For SoxS, both DStressR variants recovered increased activity under paraquat
and PMS in the three-way intersection. The paraquat response agrees with the
canonical SoxRS interaction reported by Binsfeld et al.
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. We also observed reduced SoxS reporter activity under
phleomycin, tobramycin, and tunicamycin in both model-based analyses.

For the MicF/OmpF permeability axis, we recovered the opposing
`micFp-Procaine` and `ompFp-Procaine` responses, together with increased
`micFp` activity under 2,2-bipyridyl and caffeine. These four pairs were shared
by all three analyses. Binsfeld et al. independently confirmed
caffeine-induced MicF expression and Rob-dependent changes in outer-membrane
proteins [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. With EVC calibration, we additionally
recovered the published `micFp-Paraquat` and `micFp-Vanillin` calls.

For marRAB and Rob regulation, both DStressR variants identified positive
`marRABp-Clarithromycin`, `marRABp-Azithromycin`, and `marRABp-Tetracycline`
effects and negative `robp-Clarithromycin` and `robp-Azithromycin` effects
among the shared calls. These directions agree with the published pattern of
marRAB induction and rob repression; clarithromycin-induced marRAB
expression was independently validated in the original study
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. Additional positive effects include
`marRABp-Acetylsalicylic acid` and `marRABp-Trimethoprim`. We also recovered
the published increase in `marRABp` activity under caffeine.

At the efflux reporter `acrABp`, we recovered the published increases under
clarithromycin and azithromycin. Both DStressR variants also identified
reduced activity under procaine, and EVC calibration yielded additional
positive effects under spiramycin and moxifloxacin. Rifampicin and phleomycin
produced coordinated decreases across several reporters in the total-effect
matrix. Suppl. Table 3 lists the 118 additional DStressR pairs and available
pair- or pathway-level literature annotations.

The compact screen also allowed us to fit the full promoter-by-compound interaction model
in Eq.\eqref{eq:optional-interaction-model} and compare the resulting total
effects (Suppl. Note F; Suppl. Tables 4--5; Suppl. Figures 3--4).
We further examined deviations from the seven-promoter average using the
reporter-relative effects in Eq.\eqref{eq:implemented-global-relative-estimates}
(Suppl. Note G; Suppl. Figures 5--7; Suppl. Tables 6--7).


## Analysis of an E. coli Promoter-Activity Reporter Screen

### Screen Design and Promoter-Activity Response Construction

We next considered the PFIbox promoter-reporter study of
@French2018PFIbox, which measured the Zaslaver *E. coli*
promoter-GFP library [@Zaslaver2006ReporterLibrary] in high-density colony
arrays under a panel of antibiotic perturbations. The primary signal is a
fluorescence time series acquired from colonies on solid agar. The published
workflow uses promoterless controls for fluorescence background and
constitutive reporters as image-derived biomass proxies
[@French2018PFIbox].

For colony observation $i$, let $a_i$ denote the promoter reporter, $j_i$ the
antibiotic-dose treatment level, $k_i$ the repeated colony-position index
within promoter $a_i$, and $t$ time. We write $\Phi_i(t)$ for the measured GFP
fluorescence trace, $B_i(t)$ for the matched promoterless-background trace, and
$C_i(t)$ for the matched constitutive-reporter biomass proxy, after fluorescence
preprocessing. French et al.
define promoter activity by first forming biomass-normalized fluorescence and
then taking a temporal derivative. In our notation, the normalized fluorescence
curve is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pfibox-normalized-fluorescence}
q_i(t)
  =
  \max\left\{\frac{\Phi_i(t)-B_i(t)}{C_i(t)},0\right\},
\end{equation}

for positive $C_i(t)$. We used the deposited biomass-normalized fluorescence
traces and reconstructed their unscaled smoothed derivatives. The corresponding
promoter-activity curve is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pfibox-promoter-activity}
PA_i(t)
  =
  \frac{d}{dt}q_i(t)
  =
  \frac{d}{dt}
  \left\{
  \max\left[\frac{\Phi_i(t)-B_i(t)}{C_i(t)},0\right]
  \right\}.
\end{equation}

Biomass correction enters through
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-normalized-fluorescence}. For a user-defined time window
$\mathcal T=[t_0,T]\subseteq[0,T_{\max}]$, the scalar response supplied to DStressR is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pfibox-pa-summary}
y_i^{PA}(\mathcal T)
  =
  \int_{\mathcal T} PA_i(t)\,dt.
\end{equation}

The endpoint $T$ is an analysis parameter. We reconstructed activity on the
197-sample grid retained in the deposited data by trimming the first 19
fluorescence differences before quadratic LOESS smoothing with span 0.5
(Suppl. Note H). With the five-minute acquisition interval, the retained
right-endpoint grid runs from $t_0=100$ minutes to $T=18$ hours. We integrated
these signed, unscaled activity curves by the trapezoidal rule, preserving
between-colony amplitude differences. French et al. use per-curve min--max
scaling to examine temporal expression profiles and exclude early timepoints
from clustering because low biomass can produce spikes
[@French2018PFIbox; @Zaslaver2006ReporterLibrary].

### DStressR Effect Estimation from Supplied Promoter-Activity Responses

The scalar promoter-activity summary is supplied to the downstream model as
$y_i^\star=y_i^{PA}(\mathcal T)$. Here $j_i$ denotes the antibiotic-dose
treatment level, with the untreated control encoded as $j=0$, and $k_i$
denotes the repeated colony-position index within promoter $a_i$. Antibiotic
identity groups dose levels for annotation and plotting. The repeated
colony-position index enters as a reporter-wise adjustment term because the
fixed high-density layout preserves comparable positions across treatment
plates. The reporter-wise model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pfibox-linear-model}
y_i^\star
  =
  \eta_{a_i}
  +
  \theta_{a_i j_i}
  +
  \rho_{a_i k_i}
  +
  \varepsilon_i.
\end{equation}

Here $\theta_{a0}=0$ for the reference condition, and
$\theta_{aj}$ is the treatment-level effect for reporter $a$ after adjustment
for repeated colony position. Terms $\rho_{ak}$ are
included only when at least two colony-position levels remain for reporter $a$
after filtering. When this condition is not met, repeated observations are
retained as replicate measurements for residual variance estimation without
introducing a separate fixed-effect coefficient.

The total effect for reporter $a$ and treatment perturbation $j$ is the
colony-position-adjusted coefficient
$\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)=\theta_{aj}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model}. We test changes relative to the untreated
control through $H_{0,aj}:\theta_{aj}=0$. We also examine the corresponding
reporter-relative effects
$\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathcal T)=\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)-\overline{\Delta y}_{\cdot j}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)$
in Suppl. Note H.2, using Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect} on the
promoter-activity response scale.

We fitted Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model} to the integrated responses in
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-pa-summary}. The analysis contained $M=273{,}792$
colony-level observations and $n=1{,}797$ promoters. The
perturbation set contained $p=33$ non-reference antibiotic-dose treatment
levels, corresponding to 15 antibiotic identities. Untreated observations
from 13 source arrays form the reference condition. The fitted hypothesis
family contained $|\Omega|=np=59{,}301$ promoter-treatment effects.
Thus, this application has an $n\gg p$ design, with a
large reporter library measured against a smaller set of treatment levels.

### Results

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}

**Effect-matrix estimation and diagnostics.** We first summarized response
structure by clustering the fitted total-effect
matrix $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)=\widehat\theta_{aj}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model} (@fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery a). Rows
group promoters with similar antibiotic-response profiles across the analyzed
treatment levels. We used correlation distances and complete linkage on both
axes, retaining unscaled effect sizes for display. Eight descriptive reporter
groups summarize the row hierarchy; one constant profile was excluded from
correlation clustering. Four illustrated pairs are marked in the heatmap and
shown as colony-level activity trajectories in @fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery b.

**Total-effect inference.** We next tested which antibiotic-dose treatments
changed promoter activity relative to the untreated control, using the total
effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model} and the moderated statistic in
Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue}. We observed an enrichment of small p-values
(@fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery c), with 5,101 significant promoter-treatment
pairs under a single BH correction across all 59,301 tests at FDR 0.05.
Ordinary tests identified 5,090 pairs (Suppl. Note H.1; Suppl. Figure 8).
The reporter-relative effect analysis identified 8,785 pairs, including
3,923 shared with the total-effect analysis (Suppl. Note H.2; Suppl. Figure 9).

We illustrate two positive and two negative total effects using four manually
selected pairs from a 20-pair panel combining effect magnitude, statistical
evidence, and reporter and antibiotic diversity (Suppl. Note H).
The positive `recN-Ciprofloxacin-18` effect reflects increased early activity
and agrees with the SOS and DNA-damage response reported by French et al.,
who explicitly identify `recN` among ciprofloxacin-induced promoters
[@French2018PFIbox]. We also observed increased integrated activity of the
ribosome-modulation-factor reporter `rmf` under `NalidixicAcid-18`.
Earlier promoter-reporter experiments found increased `rmf` expression during
trimethoprim-induced DNA-synthesis stress [@Bollenbach2009Cell].

![DStressR analysis of integrated promoter activity in the PFIbox screen. Panel a shows the colony-position-adjusted total-effect matrix $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)=\widehat\theta_{aj}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model}, with 1,796 reporter profiles and 33 treatment levels ordered by correlation distance and complete linkage. The symmetric color scale saturates at the 98.5th percentile of absolute effects; black circles and callouts mark the four illustrated pairs. Panel b shows reconstructed, unscaled activity curves for two negative effects (left) and two positive effects (right). Orange curves represent treated colonies, gray curves untreated references, and the darker summary curves pointwise medians. Annotations give fitted total effects and raw moderated p-values; inference concerns the integral in Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-pa-summary}. The four pairs were manually selected from the 10 positive and 10 negative examples described in Suppl. Note H. Panel c shows raw moderated total-effect p-values; blue bars mark pairs significant under global BH correction at FDR 0.05. Panel d shows the corresponding volcano plot, with antibiotic-specific colors shared across dose levels and the same four pairs outlined and labeled. The y-axis is capped at $-\log_{10}(p)=50$.](../../analysis/outputs/french_pfibox/temporal_unscaled_integral_analysis/selected_four_figure6/pfibox_clustering_and_inference.png){#fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery width="90%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="H"}

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}

We observed a negative total effect for `ompC-Ampicillin-18`, with lower
activity over the early part of the retained interval. Ampicillin-associated
decreases in `ompC` transcripts have also been reported in wild-type
uropathogenic *E. coli* [@Choi2024PorinResponse]. The negative
`msrB-Sulfamethoxazole-18` effect combines an attenuated early response with
a later decline. MsrB repairs oxidized methionine residues in proteins
[@Grimaud2001MsrB]. These four trajectories and their fitted integral
differences are shown in @fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery b; their positions
in the effect matrix and volcano plot are highlighted in panels a and d.

We also compared the eight effect-profile groups with the 12 untreated
temporal-profile clusters reported by French et al. Exact identifiers matched
1,478 promoters, with an adjusted Rand index of 0.033 (Suppl. Note H).
This comparison relates the temporal organization of untreated activity to
the organization of antibiotic-induced integral changes.

## Discussion

Applying `DStressR` across arrayed reporter datasets highlights how explicitly
separating response construction, covariate adjustment, and
perturbation-wide centering clarifies the inferential target. In the *E. coli*
promoter-compound screen, DStressR retains the reference-based logic of the
published analysis while providing a model-based response scale and tests of
promoter-compound changes relative to water
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. In the PFIbox
screen, an established dynamic promoter-activity estimator supplies the
response, and the linear model adjusts for repeated colony position before
estimating antibiotic-dose effects [@French2018PFIbox].

We also analyze the processed promoter-activity compendium released by
Kochanowski et al. (Suppl. Note I.1), where supplied activity summaries define
the response matrix and reported standard deviations support approximate
summary-level inference. Total effects and rank-1 decomposition recover the
published global growth-associated promoter-activity axis and expose residual
condition-specific structure [@Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling]. The Dash et
al. fluorescence/OD global-regulator experiment (Suppl. Note I.2) retains
paired time series, allowing response-scale estimation from the larger
no-stress reporter panel before inference in the targeted weak-stress design
[@Dash2024GlobalRegulators].

Global perturbation effects remain explicit in the fitted effect matrix. Many
chemical or stress conditions affect growth,
metabolism, reporter maturation, fluorescence or luminescence chemistry, and
global regulatory state. In such cases, the total-effect matrix and the
rank-variance diagnostic provide a screen-level view before individual hit
calls are interpreted. Reporter-relative effects are appropriate when the
scientific target is a reporter-relative response beyond the average effect of
the perturbation. Rank-adjusted total effects provide a complementary target
when a dominant structured mode is present and one asks which
reference-relative responses remain after removing that mode. These estimands
answer different biological questions.

Methodologically, DStressR follows the spirit of successful
differential-analysis workflows in genomics. As in `limma`, `edgeR`, and
`DESeq2`, the central idea is to fit many individual contrasts while borrowing
information across a high-dimensional screen for stable uncertainty
quantification and calibrated multiple testing
[@Smyth2004limmaEB; @Robinson2010edgeR; @McCarthy2012edgeRGLM;
@Ritchie2015limma; @Love2014DESeq2]. The empirical-Bayes moderation in DStressR
acts on contrast variances while preserving the response scale and the fitted
effect matrix. Diagnostic plots of effects, variances, p-values, and hit
overlaps can therefore be interpreted as different views of the same fitted
model.

DStressR fits into larger high-throughput workflows that include plate-reader
or image processing, quality control, replicate filtering, and growth-curve
summarization or modeling. Existing tools and workflows address upstream tasks,
including colony-screen analysis and microbial growth modeling
[@Kritikos2017Iris; @Doherty2023ChemGAPP; @Sprouffske2016Growthcurver;
@DGrowthR; @Angaroni2025Kinbiont; @Williams2025ChemicalGenomicsWorkflow].
Subsequent steps include annotation of significant reporter-perturbation pairs,
comparison with known regulatory modules, pathway or network visualization, and
selection of candidates for validation.

Several limitations remain. First, variance estimation for reporter-relative
effects relies on a cross-reporter independence approximation.
Technical covariates absorb broad plate-level shifts, and unmodeled spatial or
batch-level correlations may still influence variance estimates in extremely
dense layouts. Second, uncertainty from upstream growth-curve fitting is
treated as fixed input to the final test statistic.
An end-to-end time-series model could propagate this uncertainty.
Third, reporter-time-series
reconstruction methods, including regularized linear inversion
[@Zulkower2015WellInverter; @Vidal2023LinearInversion] and mechanistic Lux
models [@Iqbal2017Lux], are natural upstream extensions when promoter activity
itself is the scientific target. The PFIbox analysis also points to a dynamic
extension in which reporter-specific biomass exponents are estimated directly
from fluorescence and biomass-proxy traces before promoter-activity summaries
are passed to the effect model. Further extensions could include robust
linear-model fitting [@Huber1981RobustStatistics], hierarchical response-scale
estimation [@Morris1983EmpiricalBayes], trend-aware and robust variance
moderation [@Law2014Voom; @Phipson2016RobustEB], permutation-based calibration
for small designs [@Ernst2004Permutation; @PhipsonSmyth2010Permutation], and
joint propagation of growth-model uncertainty into differential-response
inference [@MurphyTopel1985TwoStep].

In summary, `DStressR` establishes a principled,
scalable, and reproducible statistical foundation for response modeling,
effect decomposition, and calibrated hit discovery in large-scale chemical
genomics screens.

## Availability and Reproducibility

`DStressR` is available as an R package at
<https://github.com/muellsen/DStressR/> with package documentation at
<https://muellsen.github.io/DStressR/>. The repository contains code for the
model-based analysis, the median-polish estimator, and the empty-vector-control
estimator, together with numerical tests for the reported estimators.
Supplementary Note A gives software-level workflow snippets corresponding to
the analyses described in this manuscript.
