## Supplementary Material to "DStressR enables statistical analysis and inference of large-scale arrayed chemical genomics screens" {.unnumbered}

### Supplementary Note A: Software Implementation {.unnumbered}

DStressR is implemented as an R package for reproducible analysis of arrayed
reporter-perturbation screens. The exported workflow follows the statistical
layers described in the main text. `prepare_assay()` standardizes a
long-format assay table, constructs the response, records the reference
condition, and stores the technical design. Growth exponents can be estimated,
supplied, or fixed, with a dedicated set of control-well covariates if this
should differ from the downstream model design. Matched background reporters
can be calibrated by Huber regression, ordinary least squares, or direct
subtraction. Numeric design variables such as concentration index can be
retained as quantitative covariates, while plate, batch, and replicate labels
can be handled as factors.

`fit_destress()` fits the model-based workflow and stores response metadata,
growth-exponent estimates, background-calibration estimates, model settings,
and reporter-perturbation effect-model components. `results()` constructs the
contrast-level inferential table, including test statistics, p-values, and
their selected multiplicity adjustment; `model_parameters()` exposes fitted
parameters, and `call_hits()` converts result tables into directional calls.
We use the model-based workflow as the default path, while median-polish and
Salmonella empty-vector-control presets reproduce published screen-specific
analyses and enable comparison with the model-based estimand.

Input column names are specified by the user and remain dataset-specific:
the Binsfeld screen uses the original `drug` label, and the Dash fluorescence
experiment uses a derived `stress` label. Result tables support visualization,
workflow comparison, and manuscript exports.

For a generic arrayed reporter screen without a matched background reporter,
the complete model-based workflow can be written as:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(DStressR)

assay <- prepare_assay(
  screen_table,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = "DMSO",
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_fixed_time",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "plate",
  replicate = "replicate"
)

fit <- fit_destress(
  assay,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  adjustment = "by_reporter"
)

pair_results <- results(fit)
hits <- call_hits(pair_results, fdr = 0.05, effect = "total_effect")
```

When a matched empty-vector or background reporter is available, it enters
during response construction:

```{r}
#| eval: false
assay_evc <- prepare_assay(
  screen_table,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = "DMSO",
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_fixed_time",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "plate",
  replicate = "replicate",
  background_reporter = "EVC",
  background_method = "huber",
  background_by = c("perturbation", "plate", "replicate")
)

fit_evc <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  adjustment = "by_reporter"
)
```

For the public Binsfeld data object, the source-faithful perturbation variable is
`drug`. The two water controls are supplied together and are pooled internally as
the model reference without modifying the original input column:

```{r}
#| eval: false
binsfeld_wt <- subset(binsfeld_reporter_auc, strain == "WT" & removed == "No")
binsfeld_assay <- prepare_assay(
  binsfeld_wt,
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "drug",
  control = c("Water_1", "Water_2"),
  lux = "lux_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = "estimate",
  batch = "dose_level",
  replicate = "replicate",
  growth_covariates = "replicate",
  numeric_covariates = "dose_level",
  background_reporter = "EVC",
  background_method = "huber",
  background_by = c("drug", "dose_level", "replicate")
)

binsfeld_fit <- fit_destress(
  binsfeld_assay,
  technical = c("replicate", "dose_level"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  adjustment = "by_reporter",
  interaction = FALSE
)
binsfeld_results <- results(binsfeld_fit)
binsfeld_total_hits <- call_hits(
  binsfeld_results, fdr = 0.05,
  effect = "total_effect", padj = "total_padj_by_reporter"
)
```

For the Dash fluorescence/OD example, the local workflow converts the
weak-stress condition into a `stress` column and analyzes reporter-window units:

```{r}
#| eval: false
dash_assay <- prepare_assay(
  dash_weak_stress,
  reporter = "pseudo_reporter",
  perturbation = "stress",
  control = "Standard",
  lux = "gfp_auc",
  growth = "od_auc",
  growth_exponent = stress_alpha,
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

The fitted object retains the model settings and intermediate quantities used
in the statistical analysis:

```{r}
#| eval: false
model_parameters(fit_evc)
head(results(fit_evc))

plot_volcano(
  results(fit_evc),
  effect = "total_effect",
  padj = "total_padj_by_reporter"
)

plot_response_heatmap(
  results(fit_evc),
  value = "total_effect"
)
```

Optional model extensions use the same assay object and change only the
modeling layer. For example, a low-rank background adjustment or a full
reporter-by-perturbation interaction model can be requested explicitly:

```{r}
#| eval: false
fit_low_rank <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  background_rank = 1
)

fit_interaction <- fit_destress(
  assay_evc,
  preset = "model",
  technical = c("plate", "replicate"),
  empirical_bayes = TRUE,
  interaction = TRUE
)
```

For CRAN readiness, raw-data preparation and manuscript-scale analyses are kept
outside the installed package. The package ships compact, documented public
data derived from the published *E. coli* promoter-compound screen
[@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol], together with vignettes and tests that exercise the
exported workflow. Full application scripts remain in the source repository so
that the manuscript analyses can be rerun without increasing the installed
package footprint.

\clearpage

### Supplementary Note B: Dedicated Estimator Definitions {.unnumbered}

The package also retains two project-level estimators for reproducibility of
published screen-specific analyses: a median-polish estimator and a Salmonella
empty-vector-control estimator. Both start from pre-normalized reporter responses, construct
replicate-level z-test p-values from DMSO or other reference wells, aggregate
replicate evidence conservatively at the promoter-compound level, and adjust
p-values within promoter. These estimators reproduce earlier screen-specific
workflows; the main statistical framework uses the model-based target defined
in Section 2.

### B.1 Median-Polish Workflow {.unnumbered}

The median-polish estimator follows the Campylobacter reporter-screen workflow
of @Zannoni2026CampylobacterDrugScreen. It starts from a pre-normalized response
$u_{hk}$, where $h$ denotes a promoter-library-plate-replicate group and $k$
denotes a compound or control well. In that workflow, $u_{hk}$ is the
growth-normalized luminescence summary on the log scale. If $\mathcal d_h$ is
the set of DMSO wells in group $h$, the DMSO-centered response is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-dmso-centering}
m_{hk}
  =
  u_{hk}
  -
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal{d}_h|}
  \sum_{k' \in \mathcal{d}_h} u_{hk'} .
\end{equation}

Median polish decomposes the group-by-compound matrix as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-decomposition}
m_{hk}
  =
  \eta^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \rho_h^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \kappa_k^{\mathrm{mp}}
  +
  \varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}},
\end{equation}

where $\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ is the residual used for testing. Within each
group, the DMSO residuals define the Gaussian null used for the z test,
with $\bar\varepsilon_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ and
$s_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ denoting the mean and standard deviation of
$\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}$ over $k\in\mathcal d_h$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-null}
\begin{aligned}
T_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}
  &=
  \frac{\varepsilon_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}} - \bar\varepsilon_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}}
       {s_{h\mathcal{d}}^{\mathrm{mp}}},\\
\pi_{hk}
  &=
  2\,\Pr\{Z \ge |T_{hk}^{\mathrm{mp}}|\},
  \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Mapping each group $h$ back to promoter $a$ and replicate context $t$ gives
replicate-level p-values $\pi_{ajt}$. For each promoter-compound pair, DStressR
keeps the conservative aggregate

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:median-polish-pvalue-aggregation}
\pi_{aj}^{\mathrm{pair}}
  =
  \max_t \pi_{ajt},
\end{equation}

followed by Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment within promoter. The normality of
the DMSO-centered null values can be assessed with the Lilliefors test
[@Lilliefors1967].

In the R package, the workflow can be called either directly or through the
dedicated preset:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Direct dedicated estimator
mp_fit <- fit_median_polish(
  screen_table,
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)

# Equivalent preset interface
mp_fit <- fit_destress(
  screen_table,
  preset = "median_polish",
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

### B.2 Empty-Vector-Control Workflow {.unnumbered}

The Salmonella empty-vector-control estimator follows the Salmonella
reporter-screen workflow of @Amstalden2026SalmonellaStressScreen.
It starts from a pre-normalized, median-centered reporter response $u_{ajt}$,
where $t$ indexes replicate observations, and uses a reporter strain without
promoter insert, denoted $e$, to estimate compound-specific reporter
background. For compound $j$, let $\mathcal r_e(j)$ denote the retained
empty-vector replicate observations. The empty-vector baseline is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:empty-vector-baseline}
\bar u_{ej}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal r_e(j)|}
  \sum_{t \in \mathcal r_e(j)} u_{ejt}.
\end{equation}

Each reporter observation is transformed to an empty-vector fold change,
$q_{ajt}=u_{ajt}-\bar u_{ej}$.

DMSO values within promoter-replicate strata define the null. Here
$\bar q_{a0t}$ and $s_{a0t}$ denote the mean and standard deviation of the
empty-vector-adjusted DMSO values for promoter $a$ and replicate stratum $t$:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:empty-vector-null}
\begin{aligned}
T_{ajt}^{\mathrm{evc}}
  &=
  \frac{q_{ajt} - \bar q_{a0t}}
       {s_{a0t}},\\
\pi_{ajt}
  &=
  2\,\Pr\{Z \ge |T_{ajt}^{\mathrm{evc}}|\},
  \qquad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

As in the median-polish estimator, DStressR keeps the largest replicate-level
p-value for each promoter-compound pair and applies within-promoter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The DMSO empty-vector-adjusted values within
each promoter-replicate stratum can again be assessed with the Lilliefors test
[@Lilliefors1967].

In the R package, the workflow can again be called directly or through the
dedicated preset:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Direct dedicated estimator
evc_fit <- fit_empty_vector_control(
  screen_table,
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  empty_vector_reporter = "EVC",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)

# Equivalent preset interface
evc_fit <- fit_destress(
  screen_table,
  preset = "evc",
  response = "response",
  reporter = "reporter",
  perturbation = "perturbation",
  empty_vector_reporter = "EVC",
  control = c("DMSO1", "DMSO2"),
  replicate = "replicate"
)
```

### Supplementary Note C: Empirical-Bayes Variance Moderation {.unnumbered}

We estimate the empirical prior using the scaled inverse-$\chi^2$ model of
@Smyth2004limmaEB (Sections 3 and 6.2). This prior is conjugate to the
normal-model variance likelihood [@Gelman2013BDA, Chapters 2--3].
For raw contrast variance $v_\omega$ and ordinary-test
degrees of freedom $\nu_\omega$, the working model is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-sampling-model}
v_\omega \mid \sigma_\omega^2
  \sim
  \sigma_\omega^2 \frac{\chi^2_{\nu_\omega}}{\nu_\omega},
\qquad
\sigma_\omega^2
  \sim
  s_0^2 \frac{\nu_0}{\chi^2_{\nu_0}}.
\end{equation}

For reporter-relative effects, $\nu_\omega$ is the effective degree of freedom in
Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect-df}, obtained by matching the first two moments
of a weighted sum of variance estimates to a scaled $\chi^2$ distribution
[@Satterthwaite1946; @Welch1947]. Following @Smyth2004limmaEB
(Section 6.2), we account for unequal degrees of freedom using the corrected
log-variance

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-corrected-log-variance}
z_\omega=\log v_\omega-\psi(\nu_\omega/2)+\log(\nu_\omega/2),
\end{equation}

where $\psi$ is the digamma function. Under the working model, its moments are

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-log-mean}
\mathbb E\{z_\omega\}
  =
\log s_0^2
  -
  \psi(\nu_0/2)+\log(\nu_0/2),
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-log-variance}
\operatorname{Var}\{z_\omega\}
  =
  \psi_1(\nu_\omega/2)+\psi_1(\nu_0/2),
\end{equation}

where $\psi_1$ is the trigamma function. These expressions follow from the
log-moments of the scaled $F$ distribution induced by
Eq.\eqref{eq:appendix-eb-sampling-model} [@Smyth2004limmaEB, Section 6.2].
Let $K$ be the number of contrasts
with finite positive variances and degrees of freedom. Using their sample
variance $\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_\omega(z_\omega)$, we estimate

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-prior-df}
\widehat{\nu}_0
  =
  2\,
  \psi_1^{-1}
  \left[
    \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_\omega(z_\omega)
    -
    \frac{1}{K}\sum_\omega\psi_1(\nu_\omega/2)
  \right],
\end{equation}

with $\widehat\nu_0$ capped numerically at $10^6$ when the empirical excess variance is
non-positive or the moment estimate exceeds this cap. Given
$\widehat{\nu}_0$, the prior variance is estimated as

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-prior-variance}
\log \widehat{s}_0^2
  =
  \overline z
  +
  \psi(\widehat{\nu}_0/2)-\log(\widehat{\nu}_0/2).
\end{equation}

Using the conjugate update and moderated-test construction of
@Smyth2004limmaEB (Section 3), the moderated variance and moderated statistic
are then

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-eb-moderated-statistic}
\widetilde v_\omega
  =
  \frac{\nu_\omega v_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0\widehat{s}_0^2}
       {\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0},
\qquad
\widetilde t_\omega
  =
  \frac{\widehat{\Delta}_\omega}{\sqrt{\widetilde v_\omega}},
\end{equation}

and the moderated p-value is evaluated against a working
$t_{\nu_\omega+\widehat{\nu}_0}$ reference distribution. Centered contrasts
reuse reporter-level residual variance estimates, and response calibration is
treated as fixed. The moment calculation and reference distribution therefore
provide an approximation whose adequacy depends on the design and variance
structure.

### Supplementary Note E: E. coli Response and Total-Effect Diagnostics {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: setup-supplementary-tables
#| include: false
print_compact_kable <- function(x, ...) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    cat("\\begingroup\\tiny\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{1.8pt}\n")
  }
  cat(knitr::kable(x, ...), sep = "\n")
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    cat("\n\\endgroup\n")
  }
}
shorten_hit_set <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("Binsfeld reference", "Ref", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR without EV control", "No-EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR with EV control", "EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR without EVC", "No-EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("DStressR with EVC", "EVC", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub(" + ", "+", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x
}

source_code <- function(x) {
  out <- rep("", length(x))
  out[grepl("^Binsfeld", x)] <- "B"
  out[grepl("^DStressR", x)] <- "D"
  out[grepl("^Efflux", x)] <- "E"
  out[grepl("^Kwun", x)] <- "K"
  out[grepl("^Michan", x)] <- "C"
  out[grepl("^Mar-Sox-Rob", x)] <- "MSR"
  out[grepl("^Alekshun", x)] <- "A"
  out[grepl("^Mar-Sox-Rob and efflux", x)] <- "MSR/E"
  out
}
```

We compared total-effect estimates and hit calls from the reporter-wise
models in Section 3 with those from the full promoter-by-compound interaction
model in Eq.\eqref{eq:optional-interaction-model}. We used the same constructed
responses, technical covariates, and water reference. The tested grid
contains 7 non-empty-vector promoters and 94 non-water compounds, yielding 658
tested promoter-compound pairs. Water is the reference condition. With
treatment coding, $a_i$ denotes the tested promoter for observation $i$, $j_i$
denotes one of the 95 condition levels including Water, $\lambda_{a_i}\in
\mathbb{R}^{6}$ is the promoter indicator vector, $\kappa_{j_i}\in
\mathbb{R}^{94}$ is the non-water condition indicator vector, and
$x_i\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$ contains the technical covariates replicate and dose
level. Let
$\widehat y_i$ denote the final response after growth-response modeling and,
for the EVC workflow, EVC calibration. The concrete full interaction model
fitted in this supplementary note is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-ecoli-interaction-model-concrete}
\widehat y_i =
\beta_0
+ \lambda_{a_i}^{\top}\beta
+ \kappa_{j_i}^{\top}\theta
+ x_i^{\top}\zeta
+ (\lambda_{a_i}\otimes \kappa_{j_i})^{\top}\phi
+ \varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal N(0,\sigma^2),
\end{equation}

where $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{6}$, $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{94}$,
$\zeta\in\mathbb{R}^{2}$, and $\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{564}$ contains the optional
promoter-by-compound interaction coefficients. Thus, the fitted interaction
model has $1 + 6 + 94 + 2 + (6 \times 94) = 667$ coefficients. Its auxiliary
additive fit omits $\phi$ and has 103 coefficients (Suppl. Table 4). Technical
covariate coefficients $\zeta$ and the residual variance $\sigma^2$ are shared
across promoters in the full interaction model; the reporter-wise models
estimate these quantities separately for each promoter.
The uncalibrated interaction run uses $M=5148$ observations.
The empty-vector-calibrated interaction run uses $M=5127$ observations after
response-level calibration and removal of the empty-vector reporter from the
tested promoter set.

For promoter $a$ and compound $j$, the reference-relative contrast combines
the compound coefficient and the corresponding interaction term:

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:appendix-ecoli-interaction-total-contrast}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  = \kappa_j^{\top}\theta
    + (\lambda_a\otimes\kappa_j)^{\top}\phi.
\end{equation}

We estimated this contrast using the fitted coefficients and their joint
covariance, as in Eq.\eqref{eq:total-contrast-estimate}, and tested
$H_{0,aj}:\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}=0$ using the moderated statistic in
Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue}. The full models had 4,481 and 4,460 residual
degrees of freedom without and with EVC calibration, respectively. The
estimated prior degrees of freedom were $\widehat\nu_0=232.37$ and
$\widehat\nu_0=218.95$. We applied within-promoter BH correction at FDR 0.05
in both model formulations.

The interaction models identified 132 significant total effects without EVC
and 104 with EVC, compared with 145 and 119 under the reporter-wise models.
The corresponding hit sets shared 117 and 96 pairs, and 29 pairs were called
by all five analyses, including the published workflow (Suppl. Figure 3).
Total-effect estimates were closely aligned: the correlations between model
formulations exceeded 0.999, with mean absolute differences of 0.0050 without
EVC and 0.0038 with EVC (Suppl. Figure 4). Selected pairs and their adjusted
p-values are listed in Suppl. Table 5.

DStressR calls use moderated total-effect tests and within-promoter BH correction at 0.05. The central overlap contains 29 pairs called by all five analyses.](../../analysis/outputs/ecoli_interaction_total_effects/interaction_joint_venn_plot.png){#fig-appendix-ecoli-interaction-hit-overlap width="100%" fig-align="center"}

  )

}

)]

)

\Needspace{3\baselineskip}

**Hit-calling comparison.** We tested the reporter-relative effects
$\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:implemented-global-relative-estimates} using the moderated
p-values in Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue} (Suppl. Figure 7). These effects
describe departures from the seven-promoter average (Suppl. Figure 5).
At within-promoter FDR 0.05, we identified 80 pairs without EVC calibration
and 92 with EVC calibration. The published rule identified 53 pairs, of which
35 were shared by both DStressR analyses. The union comprised 117 pairs
(Suppl. Figure 7 g; Suppl. Table 6). The remaining intersections contain 16
Binsfeld-reference-only calls, nine DStressR-without-EVC-only calls, 19
DStressR-with-EVC-only calls, 36 additional pairs shared by the DStressR
variants, and two pairs shared only by the Binsfeld workflow
and DStressR with EVC.

In the moderation step, the estimated prior degrees of freedom were
$\widehat{\nu}_0=11.45$ without EVC and $\widehat{\nu}_0=16.38$ with EVC.
The reporter-model residual degrees of freedom ranged from 626 to 652 and
625 to 646, respectively; the centered contrasts had median effective degrees
of freedom 899.8 and 906.3 from Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect-df}.
Ordinary and moderated tests yielded identical hit sets. The volcano plots
show the shared responses, and the p-value scatter plots identify
method-specific calls (Suppl. Figure 7 d--i). Promoter-specific raw p-value
histograms are shown in Suppl. Figure 6.

Panels a--c show pooled raw p-value histograms, with model-based p-values computed by Eq.\eqref{eq:moderated-pvalue}. Panels d--f show volcano plots of reporter-relative effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:implemented-global-relative-estimates} against raw p-values, with the 35 three-way intersection calls annotated and colored by promoter. Panel g shows the three-method hit overlap. Panels h--i compare Binsfeld reference raw p-values with DStressR raw p-values; grey points are all tested pairs, triangles mark pairs called only by the Binsfeld reference rule, and circles mark calls unique to the corresponding DStressR workflow.](../../analysis/outputs/binsfeld_evc_calibrated/evc_huber_discovery_summary_figure.png){#fig-appendix-ecoli-relative-discovery-summary width="100%"}

We recovered responses across the regulatory pathways represented in the
reporter panel.

For SoxS, `soxSp-Paraquat` was a prominent shared call, in agreement with the
canonical SoxRS oxidative-stress response. Additional reporter-relative effect calls
included `soxSp-Quercetin`, `soxSp-2-2-Bipyridyl`, `soxSp-Phleomycin`,
`soxSp-Tobramycin`, and `soxSp-Tunicamycin`.

For the MicF/OmpF permeability axis, shared calls included `micFp-Procaine` and
`ompFp-Procaine`, preserving the opposing MicF/OmpF response to procaine;
`micFp-2-2-Bipyridyl` retains a known permeability signal, and
`micFp-Caffeine` matches the validated caffeine response involving MicF, OmpF,
and Rob. DStressR-only calls such as `micFp-Rifampicin`,
`ompFp-Novobiocin`, and `ompFp-Trimethoprim` remain consistent with this module.
The published workflow uniquely called `micFp-Tetracycline`, `micFp-Paraquat`,
`ompFp-Clarithromycin`, and `tolCp-Azithromycin`.

For marRAB and Rob regulation, shared calls include macrolide and
tetracycline-class responses at `robp` and `marRABp`, for example
`robp-Clarithromycin`, `robp-Azithromycin`, `marRABp-Clarithromycin`,
`marRABp-Azithromycin`, and `marRABp-Tetracycline`. We additionally recover
`marRABp-Chloramphenicol` and `marRABp-Vanillin`, two known marRABp
interactions that Binsfeld et al. report as missed by their stringent
hit-calling rule [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol]. We also call
`marRABp-Acetylsalicylic acid`, consistent with salicylate-related
MarR/marRAB regulation, and `robp-Paraquat`, consistent with links between
paraquat/SoxRS signaling and rob regulation.

Efflux and compound-class responses include AcrAB-TolC efflux signals in both
the intersection and the DStressR-only set. Common calls include macrolide
effects at `acrABp`; DStressR-only calls include
`acrABp-Chloramphenicol`, `acrABp-Fusidic acid`, `acrABp-Levofloxacin`,
`acrABp-Moxifloxacin`, `acrABp-Procaine`, and `acrABp-Spiramycin`. Overall, 30
of 64 DStressR-only pairs have direct, analog, pathway, substrate-class, or
stress-regulon support in Suppl. Table 7, indicating that
many additional calls fall within the biological modules targeted by the
screen.

EVC calibration additionally yielded a `soxSp-Caffeine` reporter-relative effect call.
This pair had a small published mean Z-score and a non-significant reference
p-value. The original study's experimental validation of caffeine responses
focused on MicF, OmpF, and Rob [@Binsfeld2025PLoSBiol].

### Supplementary Note H: Additional Analysis Details and Results for the PFIbox Reanalysis {.unnumbered}

We reconstructed the unscaled promoter activity from the deposited
`constit.normalized` fluorescence matrices. For each colony, we formed the
216 consecutive differences of its 217-sample trace, retained differences
20--216, and applied quadratic LOESS with span 0.5 on the retained grid.
Dividing by the five-minute sampling interval expresses activity per hour.
For 940 complete colony trajectories from 24 promoters selected by published
cluster membership, min--max scaling of the reconstructed activity reproduced
the deposited `promoter.activity` curves to floating-point precision
(maximum curve RMSE $1.41\times10^{-15}$). The integral in
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-pa-summary} uses the unscaled reconstructed activity.
Finite constant traces contribute zero integrals and remain in the response
table.

For @fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery a, we used correlation distances and
complete linkage on both axes of the total-effect matrix. All 1,797 reporters
had fitted effects for the 33 treatment levels. One constant reporter profile
was excluded from correlation clustering, leaving 1,796 rows. We cut the
reporter tree into eight descriptive groups; labels R1--R8 follow the
top-to-bottom heatmap order. Exact promoter identifiers matched 1,478 rows to
the major-cluster assignments in French et al.'s Table S3, leaving 318
unmatched reporters. The adjusted Rand index between the two hard partitions
was 0.0325. The published assignments summarize untreated temporal profiles;
our groups summarize treatment--reference integral effects.

For the illustrative time courses, we first selected 10 positive and 10
negative pairs among globally significant total effects. Within each direction,
we ranked pairs by the geometric mean of their percentile ranks for absolute
effect size and $-\log_{10}(p)$. We selected pairs in decreasing score order,
retaining at most one pair per reporter and two per antibiotic in each
direction. We then manually chose `ompC-Ampicillin-18`,
`msrB-Sulfamethoxazole-18`, `recN-Ciprofloxacin-18`, and
`rmf-NalidixicAcid-18` from this panel for
@fig-pfibox-clustering-discovery b. Each pair has three or four retained
treated colony trajectories. Gray curves show the untreated reference
observations used by the model; summary curves are pointwise medians.

#### H.1 Total-Effect Variance Moderation {.unnumbered}

We compared ordinary and moderated tests of the total effects
$\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)=\theta_{aj}$ from
Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model}, holding the fitted coefficients and
response construction fixed. Ordinary tests yielded 5,090 globally
BH-significant pairs at FDR 0.05, compared with 5,101 under variance moderation.
The corresponding
p-value distributions are shown in Suppl. Figure 8.

![Moderation diagnostic for total effects in the PFIbox promoter-activity screen. The panels compare ordinary and empirical-Bayes moderated p-values for the total-effect coefficients in Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-linear-model}, using integrated unscaled activity responses. Dark blue marks globally BH-adjusted p-values below 0.05.](../../analysis/outputs/french_pfibox/temporal_unscaled_integral_analysis/total_effect_discovery/pfibox_pa_moderation_diagnostic_pvalue_histograms.png){#fig-appendix-pfibox-moderation-diagnostic width="85%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

#### H.2 Centered Reporter-relative-Effect Analysis {.unnumbered}

We also tested departures from the treatment-wide average using the
reporter-relative effects

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:pfibox-reporter-relative-effect}
\Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}(\mathcal T)
  =
  \Delta y_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T)
  -
  \overline{\Delta y}_{\cdot j}^{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathcal T).
\end{equation}

The moderated tests
identified 8,785 pairs under a single BH correction across all pairs at
FDR 0.05. Ordinary tests identified 8,862 pairs. The total- and
reporter-relative effect analyses shared 3,923 pairs; 1,178 pairs were called
only by the total-effect tests and 4,862 only by the reporter-relative effect
tests.

Panel a shows moderated p-values for the centered effects in Eq.\eqref{eq:pfibox-reporter-relative-effect}, using integrated unscaled activity responses; blue bars mark globally BH-adjusted p-values below 0.05. Panel b shows the corresponding volcano plot, with colors denoting antibiotic identities shared across dose levels. The y-axis is capped at $-\log_{10}(p)=50$; labels for capped points report the true uncapped value.](../../analysis/outputs/french_pfibox/temporal_unscaled_integral_analysis/relative_effect_discovery/pfibox_pa_binsfeld_style_discovery_reporters2000_perturbations100_Tall_available_treatment_replicate_scalable_temporal_unscaled_integral.png){#fig-appendix-pfibox-relative-discovery width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

### Supplementary Note I: Additional Use Cases {.unnumbered}

#### I.1 Analysis of an E. coli Promoter-Activity Scaling Compendium {.unnumbered}

##### Supplied Summary Data and Response Matrix {.unnumbered}

We next revisited the promoter-activity compendium of Kochanowski et al.
[@Kochanowski2017PromoterScaling], which measured central-metabolism promoter
activities across environmental and metabolic conditions. The public
supplementary tables used here provide processed promoter activities and their
reported standard deviations. We use these summaries to estimate
reference-relative effects and recover the published global regulatory axis.

Let $n=64$ denote the number of promoters and let $p=25$ denote the number of
non-reference conditions. For promoter $a\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and condition
$j\in\{0,\ldots,p\}$, the available data are the processed promoter activity
$A_{aj}>0$, its reported standard deviation $S_{aj}>0$, and the
condition-specific growth rate $\mu_j$. Thus, the supplied data are
$A\in\mathbb R_+^{64\times26}$, $S\in\mathbb R_+^{64\times26}$, and
$\mu\in\mathbb R^{26}$. The glucose condition is the reference condition
$j=0$. We use the supplied promoter activity on the log scale,
$x_{aj}=\log_2(A_{aj})$, with the delta-method uncertainty scale
$v_{aj}=S_{aj}^2/\{A_{aj}^2(\log 2)^2\}$. The supplied $S_{aj}$ are standard
deviations; conversion to standard errors of the reported means requires the
corresponding replicate counts. We use $v_{aj}$ as a working
response variance for exploratory summary-level analysis. The DStressR total
effect for condition $j$ is the glucose-relative promoter activity change,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  =
  x_{aj}-x_{a0},
  \qquad j=1,\ldots,p.
\end{equation}

The resulting total-effect matrix $T=\{\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}\}\in\mathbb R^{64\times25}$ from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect} contains one row per promoter and one non-reference condition per column, giving $np=1{,}600$ contrasts.

##### Total, Reporter-relative, and Rank-1 Adjusted Effect Estimation {.unnumbered}

In this summary-level analysis, we compute reporter-relative effects using an
inverse-variance-weighted condition-wide mean. Let
$V_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}=v_{aj}+v_{a0}$ be the working total-effect variance,
assuming independent condition summaries, and define normalized weights
$w_{aj}=(V_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}})^{-1}/\sum_{a'=1}^{64}(V_{a'j}^{\mathrm{tot}})^{-1}$.
The centered effect is

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-reporter-relative-effect}
\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{rel}}
  =
  \widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  -
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}},
  \qquad
  \widehat{\overline{\Delta y}}_{j}^{\mathrm{tot}}
  =
  \sum_{a=1}^{64}
  w_{aj}\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}.
\end{equation}

This contrast asks which promoters deviate from the average response to a
condition. The Kochanowski compendium also has a biologically meaningful
condition-level structure, so we inspect the total-effect matrix before and
after low-rank adjustment.

Kochanowski et al. showed that the promoter-activity matrix is dominated by a
global condition axis related to growth-rate-dependent regulation, with
condition-specific deviations for selected promoters. We fit the summary-level
workflow with glucose as reference and decomposed the total-effect matrix from
Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect} into a rank-1 background component and
a residual total-effect matrix. Specifically, for the non-reference total-effect matrix $T$, we compute the rank-1 approximation $\widehat B^{(1)}=\widehat d_1\,\widehat u_1\widehat v_1^\top$, where $\widehat d_1$ is the leading singular value and $\widehat u_1\in\mathbb R^{64}$ and $\widehat v_1\in\mathbb R^{25}$ are the corresponding left and right singular vectors. The rank-adjusted total effect is $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}=\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat B^{(1)}_{aj}$. The rank-1 DStressR perturbation score closely reproduces the first singular
vector reported by Kochanowski et al. After sign alignment, the Pearson
correlation is 0.998 and the Spearman correlation is 0.97. The same score is
also associated with growth rate (Pearson correlation 0.75, Spearman
correlation 0.88). Thus, the DStressR total-effect matrix recovers the known
global promoter-activity axis and yields a residual matrix of
condition-specific deviations (Suppl. Figure 10).

![DStressR analysis of the Kochanowski promoter-activity compendium. The panels show glucose-relative total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, the rank-1 component $\widehat B^{(1)}=\widehat d_1\widehat u_1\widehat v_1^\top$, rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$, the condition-level rank-variance diagnostic, and the comparison between the DStressR rank-1 perturbation score and the first singular-vector axis reported by Kochanowski et al. The sign of the DStressR singular vector is arbitrary and was flipped for comparison.](../../analysis/outputs/kochanowski_promoter_scaling/kochanowski_dstressr_composite_figure.png){#fig-kochanowski-effect-decomposition width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

##### Approximate Summary-Level Inference Results {.unnumbered}

The working variances yield approximate uncertainty scores for the processed
promoter activities. For any effect target
$\widehat\theta_{aj}$ with approximate variance $\widehat V_{aj}$, we form the
normal statistic

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kochanowski-approx-test}
Z_{aj}^{\star}
  =
  \frac{\widehat\theta_{aj}}{\sqrt{\widehat V_{aj}}},
  \qquad
\pi_{aj}^{\star}
  =
  2\,\Pr\{Z\ge |Z_{aj}^{\star}|\},
  \quad Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1).
\end{equation}

These normal-reference tail probabilities are conditional on the working
variance interpretation; their calibration as tests of mean effects cannot be
established from the supplied standard deviations alone. We use the approximate p-values from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-approx-test} as an exploratory ranking of reporter-condition pairs under three targets: total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, reporter-relative effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-reporter-relative-effect}, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (Suppl. Figure 11). The volcano
plots summarize the processed compendium with variance-aware scores. Total and
reporter-relative effects produce many small approximate p-values because the matrix is
strongly structured; rank adjustment yields a more focused set of residual
condition-specific promoter responses.

The panels show total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-total-effect}, reporter-relative effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-reporter-relative-effect}, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{aj}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$. P-values are approximate calculations from Eq.\eqref{eq:kochanowski-approx-test} and are used here for exploratory ranking of processed reporter-condition summaries.](../../analysis/outputs/kochanowski_promoter_scaling/kochanowski_approx_volcano_three_targets.png){#fig-kochanowski-approx-volcano width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

#### I.2 Analysis of an E. coli Fluorescence/OD Regulator-Stress Experiment {.unnumbered}

##### Screen Design and Response-Scale Calibration {.unnumbered}

We next reanalyzed the fluorescence reporter dataset of Dash et al.
[@Dash2024GlobalRegulators], which introduced an *E. coli* library of
global-regulator transcriptional reporters. GFP fluorescence and OD are
observed as matched time series. All available reporters contribute to
response-scale estimation, and downstream inference is restricted to the
weak-stress subset.

We consider four weak-stress reporters, Fur, MarA, SoxS, and LexA, measured
under excess iron, tetracycline, hydrogen peroxide, and kanamycin, with
standard growth as the reference condition. To avoid the initial reporter
ramp-up period, each time series is summarized over three post-ramp-up windows:
early, middle, and late. A reporter-window pair $\tilde a=(a,w)$ is used as the
analysis unit, where $a$ denotes the biological reporter and $w$ denotes the
time window. This
testing design contains 12 reporter-window units and four
non-reference stress conditions, yielding 48 reporter-window/stress contrasts.

For each retained well-window summary, let $F_i$ denote GFP AUC and let $O_i$
denote matched OD AUC in the same time window. We define the calibrated
fluorescence/OD response by the DStressR response equation,

\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}
\widehat y_i
  =
  \log_2(F_i)
  -
  \widehat\alpha_{a_i}\log_2(O_i).
\end{equation}

Here the exponent is indexed by the biological reporter $a_i$ and shared
across its time windows. The windows act as repeated post-ramp-up
summaries for estimating a reporter-level growth-response relationship. We
estimate this response scale from the larger no-stress growth-transition panel,
which contains 18 reporters summarized over the same three windows. Summaries
from different windows of the same trajectory are dependent. The calibration
uses them to estimate a common reporter-level slope, with an independence
working approximation for its standard errors and shrinkage weights. The
weak-stress inference then receives the four calibrated exponents for Fur,
MarA, SoxS, and LexA as supplied response-scale parameters.
In this run, the shrunken estimates were
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{Fur}}=-0.006$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{MarA}}=0.994$,
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{SoxS}}=0.251$, and
$\widehat\alpha_{\mathrm{LexA}}=0.644$.

##### Total, Reporter-relative, and Rank-1 Adjusted Effect Estimation {.unnumbered}

The total effect for reporter-window unit $\tilde a=(a,w)$ and stress condition $j$
is the reference-relative effect from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}, evaluated
on the fluorescence/OD response scale in
Eq.\eqref{eq:dryad-calibrated-response}. This estimand asks whether the
reporter-window response changes under a stress condition relative to standard
growth. In this dataset, total-effect inference is closest to the biological
question addressed in the original weak-stress experiment: whether the reporter
library responds to the stress cues expected for the corresponding global
regulators.

We first inspect total effects on the calibrated fluorescence/OD response scale
(Suppl. Figure 12, panel a). We observed a strong Fur response
under excess iron and additional Fur responses across other stresses. The other
canonical regulator-stress combinations also have positive total effects, but
they are weaker: MarA responds to tetracycline, SoxS to hydrogen peroxide, and
LexA to kanamycin.

![Effect decomposition in the *E. coli* fluorescence data. Rows are reporter-window units ordered by biological reporter and time window; columns are weak-stress conditions. The panels show the reference-relative total effect from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect} on the calibrated response in Eq.\eqref{eq:dryad-calibrated-response} (a), the reporter-relative effect $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{rel}}$ (b), the estimated rank-1 component from Eq.\eqref{eq:low-rank-background-estimand} (c), and the rank-adjusted total effect $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (d). Black boxes mark the expected reporter-stress pairs across the three time windows in panels a, b, and d.](../../analysis/outputs/dryad_global_regulators/dryad_weak_stress_windows_calibrated_alpha_rank1_effect_decomposition.png){#fig-dryad-effect-decomposition width="100%" fig-align="center" fig-pos="htbp"}

We then computed reporter-relative effects using Eq.\eqref{eq:reporter-relative-effect},
centering the total effects across the 12 tested reporter-window units within
each stress condition (Suppl. Figure 12, panel b). These effects quantify
departures from the stress-wide average response.

To examine the effect of low-rank background adjustment, we use the
reporter-window by stress total-effect matrix from the *E. coli* fluorescence
data. The Fur-dominated response forms a structured mode across reporters, time
windows, and stresses. We therefore estimate one low-rank component from the
total-effect matrix
(Suppl. Figure 12, panel c), and define a rank-adjusted total
effect before any optional centering step.

For the total-effect matrix
$T=\{\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}\}$, DStressR estimates the rank-1
background component described in
Eq.\eqref{eq:low-rank-background-estimand}. The rank-adjusted total-effect estimate is $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}=\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot}}-\widehat B^{(1)}_{\tilde a j}$. We report the unadjusted total effects alongside the rank-adjusted total
effects (Suppl. Figure 12, panel d), which ask what
reference-relative response remains after separating the dominant structured
mode. A rank diagnostic supports using a rank-1 adjustment in this dataset:
the first component explains 83.2% of the total-effect sum of squares, and its
singular value exceeds the 99% permutation reference. Biologically, this
component is dominated by the broad Fur response.

Later-window MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin effects become visible as
positive residual signals, while the first low-rank component captures most
of the Fur/iron signal.

##### Inference Results {.unnumbered}

We next attach uncertainty to the three effect targets shown in Suppl. Figure 12: total effects from Eq.\eqref{eq:total-effect}, reporter-relative effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{rel}}$, and rank-adjusted total effects $\widehat{\Delta y}_{\tilde a j}^{\mathrm{tot},1}$ (Suppl. Figure 13). Across the 48 reporter-window/stress
contrasts, 36 total effects are significant after within-reporter
Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment. The reporter-relative effect analysis calls 42 of
48 contrasts. We interpret the many small p-values as evidence for a highly
structured effect matrix with broad shared signal across the tested
reporter-window units.

After rank-1 adjustment, 30 rank-adjusted total effects remain significant.
This inference result is consistent with the effect
decomposition in Suppl. Figure 12: removing the dominant
structured Fur mode reduces broad stress-associated signal while retaining
several expected reporter-stress responses, especially later-window
MarA/tetracycline and LexA/kanamycin effects.
